The main part of the old Mount Royal division is to be known as the division of Notre Dame de Grace and if the population of Notre Dame de Grace is substantially in accord with 'the policies of this government I feel they will elect a supporter of it.
I think I should refer to another aspect of this redistribution. When I saw the report of the committee I found the municipality of Montreal West had been transferred to the Jacques Cartier division. The traditions and the outlook of the people of Montreal West were more in keeping with the section known as Notre Dame de Grace or with the new Mount Royal division as it is being set up. After I had received representations from Montreal West residents, and after consultation with the Minister of Finance I suggested to the committee that Montreal West could legitimately become part of the new Mount Roval. T'his suggestion was adopted and Montreal West will, under the setup, become part of the new division of Mount Royal which is shown on this map of Montreal.
The subcommittee of the province of Quebec has, in my opinion, made a fair and just allocation of the electors of that province, and especially in the island of Montreal. It has been a difficult task, but I will accept the recommendations as embodied in Bill No. 18.
I was going to make an appeal to Caesar this morning, but since we have no Caesar and since we have no dictator I think I will make this appeal to the government itself. My appeal will be somewhat different from the appeal of the hon. member for Lake Centre. I appeal to the government to pass this redistribution act so that the province of Quebec will have fair and proportionate representation in the new House of Commons. I appeal to the government not to allow the small differences of opinion of a few members to influence the greater decision that will give fair and just representation to our province. I appeal to the government, in the words of St. Paul's epistle to the Corinthians, chapter 15, verse 58: "Be ye stead-

fast, immovable." And I mean steadfast and immovable in justice and in fairness to the electors of Canada. When an election is called, if I have the honour to contest the new seat of Notre Dame de Grace, I will contest it as a supporter of the government and will abide by the decision given by the electors of that division.

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
I have understood from
the Prime Minister that it is not the intention of the government to yield to the suggestion that has been made to it that redistribution be done over by what it pleases some to call an impartial body. That being the case, it is probably futile to discuss the constitution of any such body. If that discussion ever becomes pertinent I shall place before the house my own reasons against the appointment of judges to such a commission. The right hon. gentleman who leads the house has indicated in no uncertain terms that he does not share my views as to the impropriety of appointing judges for the solution of quasi-political problems. I think he must concede that the appointment of judges to draw an electoral map of Canada, especially where three of the judges would be of one political stripe and three of another, would be a great misfortune and a great folly. It would be dragging these gentlemen back into the dust of an arena which they had long since escaped, and it would be possibly a reason-a reason at least in the minds of some evil minded people

for appointing a man to the bench, that he might at some later time be used for a task of this description.
I will satisfy myself by saying that if such a proposal ever comes before the house and I happen to be a member I shall resist it, as I know all lawyers and judges will resist it, and as I believe everyone who thinks well of our legal institutions, especially of our judiciary, will be bound to resist it.
The purpose of my few remarks this morning is to deal with a matter that is at least non-partisan and, I believe, non-political. In the schedule of the Quebec constituencies, the constituency of Wright has disappeared and is being replaced by the constituency of Gatineau. I said in the committee, and I repeat here-prompted by numerous protests received from people who hold this view- that it is unfortunate that a great historical name should be unnecessarily obliterated from the geography and from the official records of the dominion.
Philemon Wright was born in the year that Canada passed from the old allegiance to the new, in 1760. It is just 150 years ago this year that he established the community

out of which Ottawa has grown. He and the group of 30 or 40 people whom he brought with him redeemed this section of country from the wilderness. For over three generations the area adjacent to Ottawa on the Quebec side of the Ottawa river has borne his name.
Wright came up the river as the head of a numerous company. I find in his own language, in an article which he contributed to the Canadian Magazine in 1824, a description of that epic journey. Here are a few lines:
And in 1797 I came again to Canada and visited Quebec. I then viewed the country on both sides of the St. Lawrence, the whole of the distance from Quebec, until I arrived at the Ottawa or Grand river in the township of Hull, taking time to explore and examine the country, more particularly the parts bordering on both sides of the Ottawa or Grand river.
The next year he came with a large company of people, with horses and cattle. He cleared away the forest, he developed power on the rivers, he built mills and started the flourishing settlement of Hull and the settlement which, as I said a moment ago, later extended to this side of the river and became the nation's capital, Ottawa.
The name Gatineau is one that is well known. In fact, Mr. Wright was known in his day as the king of the Gatineau. Possibly it has another king today. Be that as it may, his was a great name, a name that should not ruthlessly be erased from our annals. Gatineau was a fur trader who, tradition says, was drowned in the river in 1680 something. His name is carried by that great river and is also borne by a provincial constituency in the province of Quebec, which however is not coextensive with the new constituency which, according to the bill, is also to bear the name of Gatineau.
I am going to make a motion, seconded by a great great grandson of Mr. Wright, the effect of which will be that the name of "Wright" will be rescued from quasi-oblivion. I would recall to the committee that Philemon Wright was a pathfinder, a pioneer, a Canadian whose story all should remember and whose example many should follow. I therefore move, seconded by Mr. Percy Wright:
That in the Quebec schedule the word "Gatineau" be deleted and the word "Wright" be put in its place opposite the figure "18" on page 21.

speechtext:
I had not intended to speak on the present bill, but after the remarks made and the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Stanstead, I think it is my duty to say a few words and to give some explanation concerning the suggested change in the name of the county from ''Wright" to "Gatineau".
If we look at this bill, there are two changes so far as my constituency is concerned. In the first place, the name of Gatineau replaces that of Wright. In the second place, some municipalities or parishes in the Lievre valley, having a population totalling 4,000 to 4,500 people which are represented at the present time by the Minister of Public Works, have been added to my constituency.
If we look back we see that the constituency of Wright was established in 1892 and was then composed of the present constituency of Wright, of the city of Hull and what is also today the remainder of the constituency of Hull. In 1924 an amendment was adopted which had the effect of dividing the constituency of Wright and forming two constituencies out of it; one named Hull, comprising the city of Hull, and what is at the present time the remainder of the constituency of Hull, leaving to Wright its actual limits under the name of Wright, territory in which, I wish to state right now, nearly everything is known under the name of Gatineau.
In 1939, the municipal council of the county of Gatineau, which comprises exactly the same territory as the present constituency of Wright, and which is composed of all the mayors of such territory, with the exception of the
mayor of Aylmer-because in the province of Quebec the mayor of a town is not a member of a county council-adopted a resolution. I think there are thirty or thirty-one members in this county council. The resolution was to the effect of requesting my predecessor in this house, Dr. Rodolphe Leduc, to ask this parliament to substitute the name Gatineau for that of Wright. I wish to mention here that this county council of Gatineau is composed of French-speaking Canadians and Englishspeaking Canadians. This motion was proposed by Mr. A. J. Earle, mayor of the town of Wakefield, an English-speaking and Conservative mayor, and was seconded by the mayor of Masham, who is a French-speaking Canadian and, I think, a Liberal. The mayors of my constituency had serious reasons to request such a change. As I said a moment ago, nearly everything is called "Gatineau" in my constituency of Wright. Those who have been in my constituency in the Gatineau district will hiave noted that. Wright is the same territory as the provincial county of Gatineau. It is also the same territory for land registration purposes and is named the registration division of Gatineau. For municipal purposes it is again the same limits, and the name is the corporation of the county of Gatineau. With the exception of the town of Aylmer, of part of the township of Hull comprising the village of Deschene and the township of Eardlev, this district which is the constituency of Wright at the present time is a district and a region which by itself is known by everybody as the Gatineau valley. If I were trying to get publicity for my constituency, I would say that, it is known as the wonderful Gatineau valley. This name "Gatineau" is so well known to designate my district that when a federal park was organized only a few steps from Ottawa and Hull, there was no question as to the name; it came naturally and it was named "Gatineau park".
While considering justly the late Philemon Wright, the founder of the city of Hull, which has not been in my constituency since 1924, as a prominent figure in our regional history, it seemed apropos to the mayors of my county-no matter to what racial group or political party they belonged'-in order to avoid confusion to request that this constituency be given the name by which it is known. I then, as dt was my duty to do, presented an official request that the name Wright be changed to that of Gatineau. Later on, only a few weeks ago, I was informed that some municipalities of the Lievre valley, having a total population of 4,500 souls, were added to my constituency. It will be agreed that it is quite natural that, I should wish to take
Redistribution

this opportunity to say that I am much honoured. by this addition to my constituency.
Although my request for a change in the name from Wright to Gatineau was made at that time, I thought then to suggest the name Gatineau-Lievre, but it would have been unfair to the remainder of the Lievre valley, the population of which is much more important than that of the portion which has been added to my constituency, to use the name "Lievre." And may I add that I did not ask to have the name changed in that way also because this part of the Lievre valley which has been added to my constituency is quite similar to that of Gatineau, not only in regard to its industries, its natural resources and scenic beauty but also in regard to the character of its origin; and the name "Gatineau" does not apply only to those living in the valley of that name but applies also to the Lievre valley, as it might apply also to many other districts, especially in the province of Quebec.
Not long ago Jean Paul Vanasse, one of our brilliant young journalists, wrote a fine article which appeared in the newspaper Le Droit, which very well expresses what the name Gatineau means to us. I should like to quote a few lines from that article, and I do so in the original French text:
(Translation):
Gatineau is a name which calls forth romantic recollections. This magic word conjures up in the minds of our grandfathers boundless and inexhaustible forests, long winters in lumber camps, the glorious era of brawny men whose axes, shining in the sun, sank into the hearts of vanquished trees. That name romantically evokes the life spent by successive generations in the Canadian forest, with its bitingly cold winters.

speechtext: It is with considerable diffidence that I rise to take part in this debate today. The hon. member who has just spoken has told something of the history of the Gatineau. I remember hearing that history, when I was a very small boy, from my grandfather, who told me not only the early history of the Gatineau but also the story of the trek from Wotton, Massachusetts, up the St. Lawrence river, when they cut the original trail across from the Ottawa to the St. Lawrence, following roughly the route of the present canal, and the establishment of the settlement on the Quebec side of the river, when there was nothing at all where Ottawa now stands. I have heard the story of the origin of Ottawa, of the first settlers who came up the following year, crossing the river and beginning the settlement on this side. It is a long story, one I should like to tell but which I am sure hon. members are not anxious to hear at this time. Naturally I am interested in seeing the name "Wright" perpetuated, and I would ask that the committee give serious consideration to the perpetuation of a name which at one time meant a great deal in this section of the country because of its historical connections with the early days. As far as possible throughout Canada I believe we should try to retain some of these old historic connections which mean a great deal now and I am sure will mean more in the future.

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
I said that I was one of the few. I know something about what a member of parliament would have to do if he is called upon to represent approximately
750.000	square miles, an area reaching for a thousand miles from one end to the other and approximately 500 miles north and south. I am sure I am not overstating it when I give those figures and I may be understating it. When I was at Yellowknife I addressed a public meeting. I just forget the name of the club, whether it was the board of trade or the chamber of commerce. This was some two or three years ago before the problem of redistribution came up. I was one of those who advised them that they should ask for representation in this house. I am convinced that if it is possible to give it to them they should have it if they want it.
The area is growing quite rapidly. I presume that there are 5,000 people more or less in the Mackenzie district covering approximately
750.000	square miles. When one enters the Mackenzie area he does so at Fort Smith, a very pretty little village of about 150 population on Slave river. I do not think I am exaggerating. I do not want to either exaggerate or understate. From Fort Smith it is almost 200 miles to the next stop at Resolution, near the mouth of the Slave river. This is not right at the mouth, you go around the mouth of the river to the west until you come to Resolution. If you are going to Yellowknife you fly across the lake from Resolution, a distance of perhaps 100 miles.
The next community if you are going northwest towards the Mackenzie river from Resolution is Hay River. I hesitate to quote any figures, but there are only a handful of people there. Then from Hay River you go to Providence where you find another handful. It is just an airport. From Providence I believe the next stop is Simpson, and then
Redistribution

Wrigley and then Norman Wells. All these places are just Hudson Bay posts. Norman Wells was a thriving little centre, but I presume since the war has ended it has shut down. Normally there would not be more than fifteen people at Norman Wells. Then the next stop is Fort Good Hope, where there is a mere handful of people, it being just a Hudson Bay post; then Arctic Red River where I do not imagine there are more than two or three white people. At that time there was just one family, a very nice family by the name of Clarke. The next stop is Fort McPherson, a very small settlement, and the next stop is Aklavik itself.
I do not think I would be in error if I said that there are no more than 5,000 people in the Mackenzie district. I think that would b* the outside limit on the number of white people in the whole area. There are a number of Eskimo and Indians and I presume those Indians who fought in the war would be entitled to vote. As I say, I think 5,000 would be the limit on the number of people in this area which the committee proposes to join with the Yukon.
It is impossible to reach the Yukon from the Mackenzie by a Canadian plane because there are no Canadian planes that attempt to fly from Norman Wells to Whitehorse. I went across in a large United States government plane and in crossing from Norman Wells to Whitehorse we passed over two mountain ranges which were perhaps 9,000 feet high. Unless you fly there is an impassable barrier between the Yukon and the Mackenzie.
The committee discussed the problem most carefully. I want to say a word abou* the subchairman, the hon. member for Grey-Bruce. I am glad to see he is sitting with the minister. In the hon. member the government has a very courteous, careful, thoughtful young man. I was greatly pleased with the work he did in the redistribution committee. I have always found him fair.
Through the chairman or by his direction communication was had with the labour unions of Yellowknife and with the council there-the government appointed at Yellowknife-and with business men in that com-mpnity. The hon. member for Skeena and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre wanted, and very rightly so, as we all dads, to ensure representation for any people who wanted to be represented. I am not- sure whether the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre communicated direct but I believe the hon. member for Skeena did, and the wires he got back were of the same import as those sent to the chairman of the committee, that they would prefer to remain as
rMr. MacNicol.]
they are until after the next census and redistribution, which will be only four or five years away, when the whole picture will be changed again. In my opinion the people of Mackenzie should be given representation of their own. The area is big enough for that, and by the time the next redistribution comes round the population may have grown to a . size big enough for representation. That is what they want. All the communications I have seen, and I saw all that were received up to the time the committee finished its work, were opposed to representation if it meant being joined up with the Yukon, and
1	saw no communications to the contrary.
The communications from the Yukon also
asked that there be no linking up of Mackenzie with the Yukon. I do not see why we should force representation upon them if they do not want it. Even if they did, where is the representation to come from, the Yukon or Mackenzie? If it comes from the one district the other will be displeased, and vice versa. To me it seems sound common sense to return to the present situation and not to put Mackenzie in with the Yukon; or else move the dividing line to the west. I looked at a map at noon. The bill says meridian 109, but if you insist on mentioning the name Mackenzie, just move the boundary from meridian 109 to meridian 135, as far as Mackenzie is concerned, and that will put a little bit of the Mackenzie area in, and that is all. I do not think that all Mackenzie should be put in. The whole proposal is silly. There is little sense to it. But if you have to do it move the boundary from meridian 109 to meridian 135. It is nothing but preposterous for this house to pass clause
2	hooking the Mackenzie area west of meridian 109 with what is now called the Yukon. It would mean that you would have an area
1,000	miles in length from east to west and 500 miles north and south. That does not make sense. There is not a member who would want- such a constituency, and it would be impossible for him to visit it unless the government financed his visits to the- area. I have been over it from end to end, both the Yukon and the Mackenzie area, right down to Aklavik and the Arctic ocean.
The committee divided three to two, and that is pretty close. It might just as well have gone three to two the other way, but it happened to be three to two for this proposal. I am going to support the amendment of the hon. member for Yukon. He has been a good and faithful member, and whether he runs again or not is neither here nor there; I hope he does, but whoever might succeed him would have to go through what he would

Redistribution
have to go through. I am sure if he runs again he will be elected whether it be for the Yukon or for the larger area. But it is an impossible position to put any member in to ask him to represent an area of half a million square miles.

speechtext: Yesterday I discussed the bill in general and gave what I thought were most convincing reasons why Mackenzie should not be added to Yukon. To me the most potent reason is that the people do not want it. By telegrams, by their representatives, by their trustees, and by their local council, which corresponds closely to a provincial legislature, they have sent in petitions against this proposal. They ask to be left as they are, even without representation, rather than have the Mackenzie district or any part of it attached to the Yukon. Why the house should insist on Mackenzie becoming part of the Yukon is something I simply cannot understand. It is not fair either to the people of Mackenzie or to the people of the Yukon. in the Mackenzie river district. So far as we know there is no settlement east of that line. The purpose of the amendment is clear. subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: I should like to say a few words on this amendment. We expect some great developments in that district in the next two or three years. We expect to ask many young Canadians to go up there and develop that country. It is a strange suggestion that we should create a situation whereby if anyone leaves any of the provinces-and it is possible that within the next three or four years as many as 5,000 young Canadians will move into that area-he should not have a vote. There will be a number of young Canadians located in both the Keewatin and Franklin areas who will be entitled to representation. I agree that it is an impossibility for any one member to represent the area which we asking him to represent there unless the House of Commons is prepared to make several amendments to the election act, amendments which will permit

It is not enough simply to pass an act and let it go at that. That is not democracy. speechtext:
There are two matters I should like to touch upon in connection with this clause. The clause reads:
The said provinces respectively shall, for the purpose of the election of members to serve in the House of Commons, be divided into electoral districts, which shall be represented as provided in the schedule to this act.
The principle of this bill was approved when it was introduced into the house some months ago. The details of the boundaries of the constituencies were left to a committee of this house to determine. The recommendations of the committee now appear in the form of a schedule to this bill. I believe it is exactly the same as the committee reported, with the exception that the government has seen fit to change one of the recommendations respecting 83166-361J	'
the representation of the city of Halifax. The committee recommended that the constituency have two single members. The government has seen fit to change that recommendation and to continue the constituency as it was before, a two-member seat.
With respect to the principle of the bill, the house has approved of it. I wish to commend the measure in one respect. It gives a measure of equity to the province of Quebec, which for some years has not had fair representation in this house. We need not go into the reasons for that. I am neither commending the failure to take action earlier, nor am I criticizing it. But this bill now accomplishes a measure of equity, and it accomplishes it by increasing the number of members in the house, particularly from Quebec. And so I commend the present bill for the achievement of that purpose.
But I criticize the bill on other grounds, and the objections all apply to clause 3. I criticize it for the unfairness it creates in many constituencies in Canada, particularly in a few. I want to deal with this feature of the bill.
Some hon. members have said that the boundaries determined for certain constituencies in Canada are the result of coincidence. The fact is that some prominent officials of this party find themselves in the position where they feel discriminated against. I feel myself that the committee is to be censured for the unfairness which has been created in certain seats, and I propose to mention them; and in certain cases I propose, when we come to deal with the details, to move amendments made to them.
The boundaries proposed of certain of these constituencies leave the impression that partisanship was apparent somewhere in the work of the committee. The seats I particularly refer to, commencing at the west, are, first, Kamloops in British Columbia; second, the Yukon, about which we have had some little discussion; third, Lake Centre in Saskatchewan ; fourth, the two constituencies of Neepawa and Portage la Prairie in Manitoba, one represented by Mr. Miller and the other by myself; and, fifth, one in the province of Ontario, namely, Muskoka-Ontario, to which has been added a large section of the constituency of Parry Sound.
I want to deal with these very briefly, but before doing so I wish to discuss one question the Prime Minister raised this morning. In discussing the procedure followed in this house in order to achieve this measure of redistribution, the Prime Minister admitted that in days past he had favoured an independent commission or committee of judges to study the matter; but he left the impression that he had had little support from the house
Redistribution

in that idea, and he referred particularly to the leader of the opposition as not having supported that view. He thus excused himself from following the policy he had formerly advocated.
Let me say that in the early days of this session I did speak on this matter in the debate on the speech from the throne. Just in order that the record may be complete, I will read the words I used. I pointed out the position the Prime Minister had taken in earlier years and asked him to make a statement when he spoke as to how the matter would be approached this time. He did' not see fit to do so. I am not suggesting that he deliberately avoided it; perhaps it was just an oversight. But later on the member for Winnipeg North Centre moved a motion that an independent committee should do this job and it was largely supported on this side of the house. I myself would have voted for that amendment, and the only reason I did not-I ask no commendation for this-was that during this session, through courtesy to the Prime Minister when he was away on many occasions, I have not voted. My own remarks may be found in Hansard of February 3, at page 54. The amendment moved by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre will be found in Hansard of February 21, 1947, and the vote on the amendment which was opposed by the government, appears in Hansard of February 24, at pages 737-38. I wish to quote what. I did say in the debate on the speech from the throne. I know the Prime Minister did not recall that I had made these statements or he would not have made the comment he did this morning. But I said on that occasion:
Now I come to the question of redistribution. As anticipated, the speech from the throne forecasts the introduction of a measure to provide for the readjustment of representation in the House of Commons. It does not indicate, however, what method will be adopted to effect this redistribution, and I should like the Prime Minister to give this information to the house when he speaks. Hon. members may or may not remember that the redistribution effected in -many will not remember these early years- 1903, 1914, 1924 and 1933 was the result of the work of special committees of this house. I assume it is the intention of the government to adopt the same method at this time.
All the indications were that that was the intention of the government.
The Prime Minister will recall that in the debate on redistribution in 1933 he strongly advocated that the task should be taken out of the hands of the House of Commons. As reported at page 5425 of Hansard for that year he said:
I am now quoting from my own remarks in the House of Commons, in which I quoted

a few lines from the statement made by the Prime Minister. This is what he said.
-"My own view ... is that redistribution should be taken out of the hands of the House of Commons, where the parties are immediately interested, and should be put into the hands of a commission of judges. I would have that commission composed of judges selected in equal numbers by both sides of the house."
I continued as follows:
I imagine the fact that the Prime Minister, and not another party, commands a majority of the house, has led him to change his mind. There are only two comments I wish to make. I hope the bill will be presented and the committee established, if such is to be the technique followed, with the least possible delay. Hon. members will not wish to have this measure rushed through by the government majority in the dying days of the session.
Those remarks were made on February 3 of this year, and I continued:
In the next place, the opposition believes that the guiding principle must be the assurance of just and equitable representation, not partisan advantage. We sincerely hope there may be general agreement on the boundaries of all constituencies. I serve notice now that we will fight to the limit any attempt at manipulation of seats designed to give an advantage to the party in power.
I imagine that if the Prime Minister had been making a speech on this matter he would have used exactly the same words as I am using. In fact, they are only different words for expressing the same sentiments as he held in the past. I continue:
The people of Canada will not take kindly to any gerrymandering which would deny them the effective voice in government to which they are entitled.
The only other observation I wish to make on the matter is this. The Prime Minister left the imp'ression that the procedure in this matter is determined by the members of the House of Commons. I suggest in all respect that the procedure is determined by the government-as it was in this case.

In closing these remarks may I add that the Prime Minister once said he favoured a judicial body to deal with matters of this kind; yet that policy has not been brought forward. At other times the Prime Minister has favoured senate reform and nothing has been done about it; and, as someone said this morning, he favoured proportional representation and nothing has been done about that. I want to read one extract from his speech and ask hon. members if what is being done here now carries out the spirit of his words. In 1937 this house was asked to consider this problem, and a committee was appointed to deal with it. That committee brought in a report after holding eighteen meetings, and in that report stated:
Owing to the shortness of the session your committee has been unable to complete its study of the methods used to effect redistribution of electoral districts in Canada and other countries, and the evidence at present before us does not warrant a final report thereon. Your committee therefore suggests that this subject be further considered during the next session of parliament.
That was in 1937. But the subject was not considered during the next session of parliament, and no action was ever taken on the recommendation of the committee in that respect. During debate on a similar measure in 1933 the present Prime Minister suggested a method previously turned down by Sir Wilfrid Laurier. At that time, as reported at page 5425 of Hansard for 1932-33, the Prime Minister said:
My own view ... is that redistribution should be taken out of the hands of the House of Commons, where the parties are immediately interested, and should be put into the hands of a commission of judges . . . selected in equal numbers by both sides of the house.
I believe the Prime Minister also read that statement this morning. I should like to quote one other brief statement by the same right hon. gentleman later on in the same debate:
... I was careful to say that my suggestion did not apply to this redistribution . . .

He was speaking in 1933, and he said his words did not apply to that redistribution. . . . when the House of Commons was again confronted with the question of redistribution . . . it would in my opinion be wise for it to adopt the plan of referring the whole matter to a commission of judges who would have the opportunity of viewing the situation impartially, not from the point of view of the self-interest of any individual member but rather from the point of view of the wider interests of the people of Canada as a whole . . .
I cannot think any Canadian would oppose sentiments of that kind. A little later the Prime Minister made this further comment:
What I proposed was a commission that would have represented on it in equal numbers judges nominated by both sides of parliament . . . Redistribution is a matter of legislation-
I want the committee to get these next words.
-but it is also one essentially of justice in the redistributing of the constituencies of Canada in accordance with principles which will be observed above all else as fair and just.

I listened to the argument with regard to that and I was particularly impressed by the observations of the hon. member for Davenport who has been more or less put forward as the expert on redistribution for the Progressive Conservative party. I heard him say in the committee that he did not see how anything else could have been done than what was done in regard to Glengarry. He said that what was done was quite in order and was quite proper. When he said that, having been more or less put forward by the Progressive Conservative party as the expert on that, I must say that I think all this talk over something being wrong in leaving Glengarry as a seat is without basis. The leader of the opposition has brought it up today knowing as he must the attitude of his distinguished colleague, the hon. member for Davenport. To me that looks like an attempt to make political capital where there is really no basis for it at all. The hon. member for Davenport is sitting right here and if what I say is not correct he can rise and contradict me. I suggest to the leader of the opposition that if he is not going to abide by the judgment of the people he puts forward to represent him on these committees, if he is going to go behind their back and attack what they did in the measured terms he used, it looks very bad to me from the point of view of political good faith.

He said that of all the unfair gerrymandering that had ever been done, what had been done in Lake Centre took the cake. He said that this was a most flagrant piece of political spite, that the practical effect of it was to make it politically impossible for the hon. member for Lake Centre to come back to this house. What is the leader of the opposition getting at? He is not saying that that is an unsound bit of redistribution based upon what a judicial committee or a judicial commission would do. He is not saying it is unfair; he is just saying that the effect of it is that the hon. member for Lake Centre can-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs

It was explained over and over again that these were only suggestions which had been laid before the subcommittee. We asked representatives of the Conservative party and representatives of the C.C.F. to come and inspect the proposals and make suggestions. I said to the hon. member for Lake Centre, "Bear in mind that we have to redistribute the whole of Saskatchewan; we have to consider that other seats besides Lake Centre are involved; you draw us a map of what you think would be right, make suggestions and they will be considered." The only suggestions of any consequence that I recall were made by the hon. member for Lake Centre had to do entirely with his own seat. With regard to the suggestions made by the hon. member for Melfort, I think practically every suggestion he made was concurred in by other members of the committee.
Now then, with regard to population. The population of Saskatchewan was 896.000 in round figures. There were eight cities, and we felt that they should have larger populations. We worked out a suggestion whereby the average city seat would have a population of 46,700, leaving the average population of the rural seats, 43,500. When we looked at the census we found that there had been a great shift in population in Saskatchewan from the

south to the north, particularly from the south to the northeast. If we were going to make a fair redistribution we had to take that into account.
We would have to change the boundaries. Furthermore, Saskatchewan was losing one seat under the constitution and we had to do something about that. That necessitated a rearrangement of boundaries no matter what the leader of the opposition may say. We looked at the census and we found, for example, that Lake Centre had a population of 34,400, which was actually 9,100 short of what it should have.
So you took a lot off.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: If the hon. member will allow me.
We have to have both sides of the story.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. member will have a chance to speak later. If I may proceed, it meant that Lake Centre was 9,100 short and we had to add to that area. We also found that Moose Jaw was 7,600 short. The only way we could increase the population of Moose Jaw, without taking from other seats which were already short, was to add something from Lake Centre. The seats were short on population. Rosetown-Biggar was 10,900 short; Kindersley was 10,900 short, so that we could not add to Rosetown-Biggar from it; Moose Jaw was 7,600 short; Wood Mountain was 7.000 short; Assiniboia was 10,100 short and Maple Creek was 9,200 short. This meant we had to add something on to the north rather than from the south or east. Anyone who looks at the map can see that. So we figured we had no alternative but to add to Moose Jaw something from Lake Centre. We could not add anything from Rosetown-Biggar. It was already short by nearly 11.000. So we proposed to add something from Lake Centre to Moose Jaw. We proposed to eliminate one of the seats in the south also to make up for the situation. In our original suggestion to the subcommittee we actually had a situation that we thought was reasonably fair. Amongst other things there had been a good part of Rosthern added to Saskatoon. I certainly hated to lose that part of Rosthern but it was felt that Saskatoon had to be brought up to a reasonable level. As a matter of fact the part of Rosthern taken off actually had a Liberal majority of 137 at the last election. The part added on to Rosthern from Humboldt had a C.C.F. majority of 306. But there had to be a real attempt to adjust boundaries on a fair basis. We confronted the hon. member for Lake Centre with these suggestions, and I a'sked for suggestions from him.

Redistribution
I should say, in regard to the increase of Rosetown-Biggar, we could not increase it in the west because Kindersley was already short by 10,900; we could not increase it to the north because the seat up there already had to have something added to it; we could not increase it to the south because that would have been at the expense of a seat already underpopulated-the only place we could increase Rosetown-Biggar was to run it to the east into Lake Centre, which was part of the picture of moving the boundaries of the seat north and east.
Actually we did not run the boundary of Lake Centre as far east as we should have done, because we did leave Rosetown-Biggar quite a bit short of the population it should have had. Had we run Rosetown-Biggar farther east than we did it would have meant running Lake Centre still farther east and north. So we thought, in order not to interfere with Lake Centre any more than absolutely necessary, we did not run the seat as far east as we should have. We left Kindersley low by 2,400 votes and Rosetown-Biggar low by 2,400 votes, in order not to interfere with Lake Centre any more than we had to. Our proposal left those two seats each 2,400 short and it still left Moose Jaw about 1,100 short. I tell this committee that that was done in order to interfere as little as possible with the seat of the hon. member for Lake Centre.
Having done that, having considered that situation-and the other members of the subcommittee know that is true as well as the hon. member for Lake Centre-the situation which we proposed left Lake Centre at 43,100.
On what census?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
At the 1941 census, the one we are going on. That was 400 under the average.
Something has been said about Melville. Our suggestion would have made Melville 43.300, which is about the average, and 200 over Lake Centre as originally proposed.
I have dealt with why we added parts of Lake Centre to Rosetown-Biggar, but still leaving it 2,400 short, and why we added some of it to Moose Jaw, but still leaving it 1,100 short. I put the question, where else could you have added from Rosetown-Biggar to give it the requisite population?
We found that Melville at the last census had a population of 47,100, which was 3,600 over what it should have. Yorkton had 50,300, which as anyone can see was 7,000 over what it should have. Humboldt had 43,300 at the last census. It meant that we had to add on to Lake Centre part of Yorkton and Melville
to bring it up to a reasonable level. Humboldt, after adding from Mackenzie to bring it down to the proper level, had 46,400, which was 3,100 over the average. So those seats to the north, Melville, Yorkton, Mackenzie and Humboldt all had several thousand over what they should have, and the seats to the south and the west, even with the additions, were still under what they should have. On the face of that does the leader of the opposition say that we should have left the seat of the hon. member for Lake Centre where it was before, and left those seats to the south and west away underpopulated, for example, left Yorkton at 50,000 in order that he might get elected? Then the opposition say they want a judicial commission to settle the redistribution! I venture to say that no judicial commission would ever have given the consideration that we gave to the hon. member for Lake Centre, and I am going to prove that.
At the 1941 census Lake Centre had 34,400. As I say, we took 1,700 off and added it to Rosetown-Biggar. If anybody thinks that that injured the hon. member for Lake Centre he should look at the last election results. The C.C.F. had a majority in that piece we took off Lake Centre and added to Rosetown-Biggar of 174. That is one way in which the hon. member for Lake Centre is terribly damaged, of course!
Next we proposed 'to take 5,500 off Lake Centre and add it to Moose Jaw. According to my figures the C.C.F. majority in that piece was 54 over the Conservatives. I do not suppose that the hon. member for Lake Centre was so terribly damaged by having that area taken off where the C.C.F. had a majority of 54 over the Conservatives.
Then we added one township and Watrous to Rosthern.

You removed
Watrous.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
We had to take territory
from Rosthern to add it to Saskatoon.
Oh!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
I do not know why that
is funny. We were drawing a map for the whole of Saskatchewan. Having added a part of Rosthern to Saskatoon we proposed to add a piece to Rosthern. That was two townships with 1,600 people. We added on from Melville 5,300, from Yorkton, 8,500, and from Humboldt, 3,700, leaving Lake Centre at 43,100, or 400 under the average. It was necessary to bring Lake Centre up to where it should be. The places that were added from Lake Centre to Moose Jaw and Rosetown-Biggar, were still under what they should
Redistribution

be. The first suggestion of my hon. friend was that Watrous township and one of the townships which had been added to Rosthern from Lake Centre should be given back to him. That first suggestion was agreed to by the hon. member for Melfort and myself. That cut down Rosthern more than it should have been. However, in order to accommodate the hon. member for Lake Centre we agreed to it. That cut Rosthern from 44,000 to 42,400, which was 1,100 under the average, but we did that to accommodate the hon. member for Lake Centre.
The next suggestion of the hon. member for Lake Centre; we had proposed- to take seven rows of townships from Yorkton and he suggested that we should take only six and put one township back into Yorkton. That raised Yorkton to 49,000, which was 1,500 over what it should have been. But again, in order to accommodate the hon. member for Lake Centre, the hon. member for Melfort and myself agreed to that suggestion.
Very generous.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
You may think it was not generous, but it is more than a judicial commission would have done.
We come now to the third suggestion of the hon. member for Lake Centre, which was that we should put back into Lake Centre practically half of what we were going to add to Moose Jaw. I remember the words of the hon. member for Lake Centre. He said, "I want to be fair about this thing." He said, "put half back again." He cannot deny he said that. Although that was going to leave Moose Jaw under what it should have been by 2,700, the hon. member for Melfort and myself said to the hon. member for Lake Centre, "All right, we will put half of this original area back into Lake Centre, although it cuts down Moose Jaw by 2,700 and leaves it 4,300 short." So far as 1 knew that is all he wanted in that regard. He felt it was fair to have that taken from Moose Jaw and added to his constituency. He said he wanted to be fair and that is what he asked for. That is the third suggestion.
His fourth suggestion was to put back into Humboldt nine rows of townships, taking from Lake Centre 3,400 voters and leaving Lake Centre at 41,000, which would have meant that Lake Centre was under what it should have by 2,400, and would leave Humboldt at 49,800 or 6,500 over what it should have had. The hon. member for Lake Centre wanted us to add to Humboldt an'area which would give that constituency 6,500 over what it should have and cut his constituency away below

what it should have had. At that point the hon. member for Melfort and myself began to think that perhaps-

Oh, oh.
Mr. TLCIvER: -we would likely be accused of doing a little too much gerrymandering for the hon. member for Lake Centre.
Hear, hear.
Did he ask for election by acclamation?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: The hon. member for Melfort took the attitude that he could not agree to a proposition which was so flagrantly gerrymandering the situation in order to help the hon. member for Lake Centre. Well, I was trying to keep peace in the family.
That is a new role.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Therefore I made a
suggestion-
You are getting old.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: -which is number five. I made the suggestion that we put tihe western part of -these townships into Lake Centre and the eastern part -into Humboldt-four of the townships into Lake Centre; -in other words put six into Humboldt and four into Lake Centre, or a sort of fifty-fifty split. Remember, the hon. member for Lake Centre did not want the whole ten. We were giving him only four out of the -ten. A great deal of argument ensued on -that. That would -have left Lake Centre 600 under what it should have had and would have left Humboldt with 5,500 more than it should have had. I talked. As I said, I tried to keep peace in the family. I talked and talked. Finally I appealed to the hon. member for Melfort. I said, "You know, if you do not give the hon. member for Lake Centre what he wants there will be a big row in the house." Finally the hon. member for Melfort, with, I could see, a great deal of doubt, said, "Well, if the hon. member for Lake Centre will agree to this I will go the length you suggest in order to get agreement in Saskatchewan," which would be som-e-thing worthy of commemorating. We all agreed to that. I said, "If we are in agreement let us sign the agreement so that there will be no argument about it." I signed my name to it; the hon. member for Melfort signed his name t-o it and the hon. member for Lake Centre signed -his name to it.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No.

No.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: There is his signature on the agreement. Can anyone-
Read what the agreement says.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: It is the schedule to this bill. After it passed the main committee I handed it over to the printer as signed. Here is the situation, Mr. Chairman. Pour suggestions were made which did, I am a little ashamed to say, more or less gerrymander things in favour of the hon. member for Lake Cerutre. But we did that knowing he was the only Conservative member in Saskatchewan, and he kept saying that he could not get elected unless we did something.
Oh, oh.
Mr. Chairman, I do not mind the bon. gentleman being generous in bis treatment of the truth, but that statement is unequivocally false.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: What statement? The document speaks for itself.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: I do not know to which statement the hon. member is referring. I suppose he does not deny his own signature.
I do not.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: I suppose he does not deny what his leader has just said. He said that unless a change iwas made the hon. member for Lake Centre could not get elected. That is, in effect, what I just said, and that is what his leader said a while ago. I suppose his own leader took it from the bon. member for Lake Centre that he could not get elected unless a change was made. That is what his leader said just now. That is the story we have heard continually from the hon. member for Lake Centre. He is an old friend; he is the only Tory left in Saskatchewan, the last of the Mohicans, as they say.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: We accepted three of his suggestions and we went more than half way to accept the fourth. He was so well satisfied that he signed it, and then we have the speech of his leader-

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: This afternoon.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: -who said that it is a most flagrant piece of political spite. But the hon. member signed it himself. I must admit that I do not understand such political tactics.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Tory mentality.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
It goes beyond anything that I can understand. He says that of all the unfair gerrymandering that ever took
place this takes the cake. Does he mean that we gerrymandered it- too much to help out the Tory member for Lake Centre, which is the only way any gerrymandering whatever took place? There is the situation, Mr. Chairman. I place the facts before the committee and I say this: I can assure the committee that in the original map which we laid before the subcommittee our idea was to try to arrange these seats on a fair basis. The suggestions made by the member for Melfort were agreed to with the consent of the member for Lake Centre and the suggestions made in regard to Lake Centre seat were acceded to in the manner I have stated. I leave it to this committee as to whether we did not treat the member for Lake Centre fairly and more than fairly.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: He said so himself.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Taking what the member for Lake Centre agreed to and signed as the fair thing to lay before the committee, and which I laid before the committee as the unanimous recommendation of the subcommittee from Saskatchewan, it is not fair to that committee, it is not fair to parliament, to have a subcommittee set up, agreeing to something like that, and then have that made the basis of such an attack as was made by the leader of the opposition this afternoon.

As the third member of this very contentious committee from Saskatchewan, who thought they had made a unanimous report, I think it my duty to say a few words on this subject. In the first place, this discussion simply strengthens the argument that we have made all along in this group, that this matter should be taken out of the control of members of parliament. Anyone who has read the debates on this particular bill as it has come before the Canadian parliament over the last sixty or seventy years cannot help agreeing with that. Time after time, whoever was in power slit the other fellow's throat at every opportunity. The other fellow howled to high heaven about it and when the position was reversed the same thing took place again.
Coming to Saskatchewan, the government were in a rather precarious position trying to make a redistribution there. They did not have much support left there, with two Liberal members and one Conservative. One of the Liberal seats had to be strengthened, and as it lay alongside a Conservative seat there was only one thing that could be done. They had to make a choice and1 they made a choice. They strengthened the Liberal seat at the expense of the Conservative seat. What would the Conservatives have done had they
Redistribution

been in power? We would have found exactly the same thing in reverse. I listened in committee to arguments made by various members of the Conservative group. I listened in the subcommittee also. No one seemed to be particularly interested in the people. Everyone was interested in his own personal interest, in his own personal seat, and 'he wanted to be sure of that. That was the first consideration and after that they tried to divide up the population.
The hon. member for Rosthern has said we drew this map. We did not draw the first map. I do not know whom he was talking about when he said "we". It was certainly not the subcommittee. When we first met we were presented with a map, and the different meetings of the committee were very short and to the point. I agree with what the hon. member for Rosthern has said with regard to the negotiations that took place in that committee. What he has said is, I believe, a correct interpretation of the various negotiations that took place in that committee. They did not meet for a very long period but in substance those were the agreements which were reached.
As the member for Rosthern has said, the member for Lake Centre did not appear to be very much interested in any other part of Saskatchewan than his own constituency. In the proceedings in the committee he raised only one point that I can remember with regard to any other constituency and that was with reference to Melville, adding an area south of Qu'Appelle valley to that constituency.
If that is the basis on which we are to deal with redistribution, the personal interest and personal preserves of individual members, I do not think we can ever reach fair decisions, and that apparently was the basis on which this matter was considered.
As I have said, regarding the divisions in the province of Saskatchewan, the original map, as far as population was concerned, was the best division made in any province in the dominion. It was the best representation by population. There were no constituencies with under 40,000 and none with over 47,000 except the city of Regina, which was left the same as it was before.
With regard to Saskatoon, on the east side of that city it was necessary to add something to the constituency of Rosetown-Biggar and naturally Saskatoon had to get some population from some other area. That was .taken quite conveniently from the constituency of Rosthern on one side and taken in such a way as one would expect from a Liberal government when they were making the 
redistribution to strengthen their position. And it did strengthen their position as far as Saskatoon is concerned.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: The hon. member will admit it took an area in which there was a Liberal majority out of the seat.
There was only one safe Liberal seat in Saskatchewan, apparently, on the basis of the 1945 election, although I would not admit today that it would be a safe Liberal seat.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Doubly safe now.

You could take a little out of it provided you got in some more afterwards that was also safe, which was done. That was the basis on which the redistribution was made in Saskatchewan.
I will say this. The Liberal party, in arranging the redistribution, took one thing into consideration first, and that was the fact that they had to strengthen one seat, and they worked everything else around that. The Conservatives, from what they have said in the committee, would have done the same thing. If a Conservative seat had been in danger they would have worked the province around it, irrespective of whatever else might take place.
As regards moving population from the south to the north, that is quite right and the only seat that could be taken out was a seat in the south. We in the C.C.F. knew that was a C.C.F. seat, but we agreed to it because it was the reasonable thing to do.
In the western portion of the province, the division between Swift Current and Maple Creek constituency ran in the original drawing north and south instead of east and west. We suggested that the natural way for the division to run was east and west, since both the railroads and the roads run in that direction and the constituency could be served better if divided in that way. The member for Rosthern agreed to that and so did the member for Lake Centre and that change was made.
The other changes suggested by myself were largely, in fact all, changes which would make for the convenience of the people who were voting. In the original map the lines were drawn on township and range lines. In sqme instances these township and range lines did not take cognizance of the geography in the area to serve the convenience of the people across rivers where they would not have an opportunity of getting to the polls without going miles out of their way. I made suggestions so as to meet the convenience of the

Redistribution
people in various areas and the chairman of the committee agreed to them and those changes were made.
To sum up, are we going to continue this way of making the redistribution in Canada? I do not think it is fair. I do not think we are strengthening our democracy. Whether we realize it or not, we cannot afford to weaken democracy in Canada. We have seen other countries which claimed to have democracy and claimed to have constitutions leave those constitutions in such a position that they could not be operated. We in Canada cannot afford to leave our democracy in such a position that it cannot be operated fairly for all the people of Canada. I think it is time that we made the necessary changes to give effect to that purpose.

I have listened with a great deal of interest to what the hon. member for Rosthern had to say, and the recital he made in connection with redistribution in the province of Saskatchewan. First, may I say this to him. At no time was there any consent. Finally on the last day in the subcommittee-andi the total period during which we ever met during that subcommittee, for all the meetings, did not exceed forty minutes-the hon. gentleman said, "Well, we will sign this as our report". When I demurred at signing it as our report he said, "Well, if you don't, you will get everything we had first for you; either accept this as the report or we shall give you what we originally had for you". That, sir, -was the statement made by the hon. member for Rosthern.
Now I intend to deal in general with certain of his remarks. Throughout his attitude was-and I take it that he was not speaking for himself alone-that first and foremost twenty-four miles on the westerly end of Melville constituency were to be added to Lake Centre.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Because they had too big a population already.

Oh, Mr. Chairman,
there never was any question about population in that.

speechtext: Oh, yes.

My hon. friend has repeatedly found himself in a position in which he had to do what he did not desire to do, but was ordered to do it by his dictator in the province of Saskatchewan. To such an extent is that so that so far as Saskatchewan is concerned this is known as the "Jimmy-mander." speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: How many?

My hon. friend
from Rosthern said that no considerations regarding votes should be before this committee. I place before him what the Prime Minister said in 1933, when he went into detail.

speechtext: That is the thanks I get for acceding to the hon. member's suggestion.

Such willingness to be led by me, a humble member in the minority, is indeed a tribute to my powers of. advocacy against a heart as adamant as his. Sixteen townships are added from Melville. Is it only coincidence, Mr. Chairman, that the Minister of Agriculture, instead of having a majority of twenty-four-

The people of Halifax.

The people made the decision announced on Friday by the hon. member for Halifax, that the committee report was not going to be accepted by the government? I would ask the Prime Minister to explain this. When was that portion of the report of the committee changed? Did he have no knowledge that it was going to be changed? Today I am not arguing that any addition be made. I am not arguing against the additions in Yorkton and Melville. I say add them on if you wish. All I object to, and what I will continue to object to, is the knob placed on the top of the constituency, abstracted from Humboldt. My hon. friend can explain it all he will, but the people of Saskatchewan will realize one thing, as the Prime Minister said in 1933; that you cannot add parts to a constituency to give it the appearance of a crossword puzzle without the suggestion that there has been a gerrymander. As far as Yorkton is concerned I have no objection to the addition, though the adverse majority may be tremendous. I have no objection to the addition from Melville, where the adverse majority also may be tremendous. All I ask is the return of the south- end of the constituency, which has always been in Lake Centre. I am not here for the purpose of bargaining, but if you say you will not restore that southern end, then the only thing I ask is that these three townships, which cannot affect the result in any way, be restored to Humboldt. In their present position, as I have pointed out on previous occasions, they are not on any line of railway which in any way goes through Lake Centre.
I have many good friends in the area my hon. friend is talking about, but I was just wondering why he thinks I should represent so many more people than the average.

I do not ask that. I say the area should be restored which was removed. The hon. gentleman wanted to be sure that wherever there was a majority it would be removed. Return to Lake Centre
what belongs to Lake Centre. These people have always been in that constituency or its predecessors.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That is what happened in 1933.
I was not here then. It is a type of political butchery, and that is all it is.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That is what we got in 1933.

Yes, and you successfully appealed to the Prime Minister of the day in 1932. If necessary I will read some of the appeals made at that time by the present Prime Minister. When the unfairness was made apparent a change was brought about. All I ask is that this northern area which is in no way connected with the constituency of Lake Centre, never having been in either^Long Lake or Last Mountain, be taken out; and there will be no argument at all about adverse majorities anywhere else. I make this appeal at this time; and I say to the Prime Minister the excuse he gave this morning, that he had nothing to do with it and that he could not possibly have this matter looked into in any way, is not good enough. I recall to his memory that he made a similar request to mine of the then prime minister in 1932, and as a result he got justice.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: We were here and you were not. In 1933 we saw the dirtiest Tory butchery that Canada ever saw.

I was not here, but Hansard was and is; and I read from Hansard at page 5561, after the present Prime Minister pointed out that an additional twelve miles would be added to the southern end of the constituency, altering the tentative southern boundary to that extent. This is what the right hon. gentleman said on that occasion:
Mr. Chairman, for the time and trouble which the right hon. the Prime Minister and those associated with him have given to the matter of the readjustment of the boundaries of Prince Albert constituency, I should like to thank them. I appreciate what has been done, although it is far from meeting the views which I expressed as to what I thought would be fair and just.
Redistribution

Nevertheless it is a change for the better as compared with the boundaries of the constituency as contained in the original report of the special committee to this house . . .
Later on the right hon. gentleman again extended his appreciation. In 1932 the boundaries of Prince Albert were agreed upon by the committee on which the representative of the Liberal party at the time was Mr. Totzke, the then member for the constituency of Humboldt. When in the House of Commons he was faced with the argument that he had consented to what had taken place his answer was: Consented?-
Always I was more or less threatened with the suggestion that if I did not agree to the proposals made by the hon. member for Regina they would be put through anyway, and possibly would be worse than before.
He accepted; but when the matter came before the House of Commons the present Prime Minister made a speech. As an example of political propriety as between persons opposed in political life it was a masterpiece, something that could be read by every hon. member of this house with advantage to himself and to the house. As he has said over and over again, we face one another across the floor of the house, but we do not lose admiration for men who disagree with us. We do not endeavour to destroy them; we argue our point of view. Perhaps one disagrees with much that the Prime Minister does, but in this country one forms an abiding appreciation of what democracy means; that men with opposite points of view can stand up and express those points of view strongly, yet still regard the other man as worthy of consideration. Sir, we do not have in this country a system of liquidation; but do we have a subtle form of liquidation whereby those who disagree, those who attack, those who discharge their responsibilities as members of an opposition shall in consequence be denied that fairness which the Prime Minister himself said in 1932 was of the essence of public life?
I have no apology to make for what took place in that committee. I care not about the overwhelming majority that is added to Lake Centre constituency which may be against me, but I do submit that there is nothing in fairness or justice which justifies the adherence of those three northern portions to Lake Centre. I have said the last I am going to say. My right hon. friend said today that he was not Caesar. There was no suggestion in my words that he was. He was quoting from someone else in 1932 and I quoted him. We all realize that the decision as to what will be done, as to what 'political opponents will be rejected, eliminated or liqui-

dated, rests finally, not with the membership of this house but with the majority represented by the Prime Minister of this country. It is not going to matter what happens to the hon. member for Kamloops, it does not matter what happens to the leader of this party or to the hon.. member for Musboka-Omtario, but in the years to come it is going to matter when it is realized that on this occasion there was an opportunity given to the Prime Minister to stand for the principles which he has epitomized and represented through years of public life.
He says that- he is not responsible. True, he did not make recommendations to the committee. But, sir, my final words are these. He did not make recommendations. However, one of the committee recommendations has been changed and I ask if it is not fair that another one be changed. I do not ask that it be changed as far as the fourteen townships are concerned; I ask only that it be changed in connection with three townships which cannot be represented without great difficulty when attached to Lake Centre.

Mr. Chairman, the letter that came from the hon. member for Champlain speaks for itself. Answering the -remarks of the 'hon. member this morning I must tell the committee that I was asked twice at the end of March by the hon. member for Champlain to go to his room. Mr. Chairman, as you say I am speaking on a question of privilege. He asked me to be a good Liberal and I told him, "Listen, my friend, I am a man who respects his own commitments. to 'the member for Laval-Two Mountains some words which I never said about a colleague. This 9hows what an insulting speech it was concerning me.
I have only one thing in this world, and that is my honour. It is the most precious of all. I know that all hon. members of this house, Liberals, Conservatives, Social Credit and C.C.F. are ready to defend their honour because honour is the most precious thing any man may have.
