speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: May I remind hon. members that [DOT] the committee has carried section 1 and section 2. It was agreed that a general discussion would be allowed on section 1, but we are now discussing section 3. Hon. members are familiar with the rules which set out that all discussion in committee must be directly relevant to the section under consideration. I hope hon. members will observe that rule from now on.

Mr. Chairman, after listening to the very sanctimonious speech of the future former member for Lake Centre, after listening to the charge made by the hon. members for Vancouver South and Muskoka-Ontario of gerrymandering, after listening to the speech made by the former premier of Manitoba, the eleventh leader of the Progressive Conservative party in Canada, that gerrymandering was done principally in the province of Manitoba by the subcommittee, I feel it my duty to give the facts to this committee.
Since the debate commenced yesterday morning particular reference has been made to four seats. One would be led to believe that the boundaries of four seats of Kamloops, Muskoka-Ontario, Lake Centre and Neepawa were guaranteed by the British North America Act, that that act guaranteed that the boundaries of those seats would never be changed at any time and that the four present members representing those four seats would be reelected at all times above the will of the electors of Canada or even above the welfare of the state.
When the charge was made by the former premier of Manitoba that in connection with his seat-he never referred to Neepawa; he referred to Portage-Neepawa, but he was referring to his own seat of Neepawa-there had been gerrymandering, that was absolutely
untrue. As chairman of the subcommittee for the province of Manitoba I take full responsibility for having outlined the new boundaries for Manitoba constituencies in the next general election. We had to lose one seat in Manitoba. Surely the former premier of Manitoba knows his province well, and when he states that the seat, of Neepawa should have remained as it was after the last redistribution he must know that that would have affected all the seats between his present riding and the Saskatchewan boundary: first of all Souris, which is the Glengarry of western Canada, one of the smallest electoral ridings in the west, and represented by a Progressive Conservative; also the constituencies of Brandon, Marquette and Dauphin, All these seats would have had to have a much smaller population and it would have been impossible therefore for the Manitoba subcommittee to bring in a report based on representation by population.
It will be noted that in Manitoba the smallest seat, Souris, represented in this house by a Progressive Conservative, has the smallest population, roughly 22.000. Every small seat in Manitoba is represented in this house by a Conservative member. The constituency in Manitoba which has the highest population at the present time is Selkirk, with 56.000.
I was given carte blanche by my colleagues from this side of the house to draft a plan which would be. acceptable to the subcommittee on Manitoba and finally acceptable to this House of Commons. Knowing well the province of Manitoba, I immediately took the * view that there were two phases of the redistribution of seats in any province, one political, and the other the principle of representation by population, The latter was chosen by the subcommittee for Manitoba. That meant that every seat, rural as well as urban, should so far as possible have equal representation by population in the next general election. That applies to the sixteen seats for Manitoba which are guaranteed by the amendment to the British North America Act.
As a result of the committee's work, all the rural ridings in Manitoba have a population of 40,000. Yet the Glengarry of western Canada, Souris, which is still the smallest seat in western Canada, was increased up to 27,240, but no mention was made of that by the leader of the Progressive Conservative party. His main complaint, which was taken up by the official organ of the Progressive Conservative party in the city of Winnipeg, the Winnipeg Tribune, was that the subcommittee on redistribution for the province of Manitoba had been guilty of political monstrosity.
Redis tribution

We amalgamated two Progressive Conservative seats, Neepawa and Portage la Prairie. But over and above that, two other seats were combined, Lisgar and Macdonald. So that if there was any gerrymandering done in Manitoba it was done at the expense of the Liberals, because the seat of Macdonald was wiped off the electoral map of Canada, and that seat is now represented in this house by a man who has served his country well during the seventeen years he has been here and who today holds the position of chief whip of the government party, a record which the hon. leader of the opposition still has to achieve in this house.
The present riding of Portage-Neepawa, as it will be known when this measure goes through, makes it a safer seat for the leader of the Progressive Conservative party-I mention this because he has spoken politically about the situation-than his present seat, because I took a block of Tory votes from Portage la Prairie and added them to Neepawa. So, df tihe Progressive Conservatives can once get the confidence of the electors they should be able to assure themselves of a representative in the next parliament. But judging by the results of the by-election in Halifax yesterday and by the attitude of the Progressive Conservatives in this house, which I may say I have observed carefully ever since I entered parliament, and having observed what I would call the lackadaisical attitude of the present loyal opposition which has abandoned the ideals of the great party they represent, and knowing that they have not lived up to their responsibilities-
Order.

If the hon. member will listen it will not hurt his education. I was saying that the Progressive Conservative party have failed to present in this house the real, true sort of opposition which one would expect under our democratic system, and that i3 not a good sign, if I may say so, Mr. Chairman, for our country. If we are to judge from the results of the Halifax by-election yesterday, where the Progressive Conservatives had 6,000 casualties as compared with the 1945 election, which party is likely to be the loyal opposition after the next general election? If democracy is to be preserved in this country I still stand by the statement I have made in the past that a return to the two old parties is essential and is desired by the people of Canada, but a wholly different attitude will have to be taken by the present members of the Progressive Conservative party if they wish to gain the [Mr. Viau.l
confidence of the people of Canada. If not, their attitude will tend to an increase of socialism in this country.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
On a point of order,
Mr. Chairman, if the hon. member is permitted to engage in this kind of partisan discussion the same privilege should be accorded to others. I do not want it, but if it is to be permitted, the same opportunity must be open to the rest of us.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I quite agree with the hon. member. The discussion at this time is not strictly in order.

Very well, Mr. Chairman.
The work done by the subcommittee on redistribution for the province of Manitoba ensures that the rural ridings of Manitoba will have a fair representation by population, all of them being in the 40,000 bracket, and the four urban seats will also be well balanced, with a population of between 55,000 and
60,000.

Mr. Chairman, I shall detain the committee for a very short time, but I want to lay before the government and the Prime Minister in particular one or two matters that I think are germane to the present discussion. I am one of the few, I think, who have spoken in this debate who are not personally affected by this redistribution, and perhaps, because of that, I am capable of speaking with some degree of detachment on this matter and may be able to impress upon the government and the Prime Minister the thought I have in mind. This must be quite an education to others besides myself who are going through a debate with respect to redistribution for the first time in our parliamentary careers. From time to time I have read the other debates, but I have never had any experience with a redistribution bill until this particular occasion. I say to you, Mr. Chairman, that this afternoon I have no desire to discuss the whole question in general. It seems to me that there has been an extended discussion on the general phases of the redistribution. I want to confine my brief observation to the constituency of which we have heard1 a good deal up to the present time, namely the constituency of Lake Centre in Saskatchewan.
I suppose it could be argued, perhaps it has been argued and it will be argued', that things have happened in previous redistributions which could always be brought up to the advantage or the disadvantage of people on both sides of the house. I fancy, however, that most hon. members, particularly new members who have come in in more recent days, will

Redistribution
want to see that whatever is done in this parliament is somewhat of a departure from the old days which at times were characterized by circumstances that we would! not want to repeat in this day and generation. That i's no reflection upon hon. members of the past, but conditions have changed and the public conscience today is much more tender, much more easily offended when it comes to representation than it has ever been before in the history of Canadian public life.
When I have been talking to men and women, people who are not interested in any way in who is elected, or the personalities or the boundaries of constituencies, they have said to me, "Is everything quite right with respect to redistribution down in Ottawa? Is any move being made to change certain seats which are represented by prominent, aggressive, active and valuable men in the opposition?" In looking at the matter from a detached point of view, I must confess I think the public conscience will be offended-and I say this with every bit of sincerity that I can summon to my command-unless the Prime Minister and the government undertake to review at least two or three of the major points which seem to stand out like a sore thumb on an otherwise healthy hand', and to try if possible to find some middle way by which the people across Canada will say that at last this parliament did not follow the precedent set by its predecessors during the years and that this government and the Prime Minister himself have met that movement and corrected some of the major defects.
I want to say to the Prime Minister at this time that there is a special reason for it as I see it. I do not think we can allow the feeling to go across this country, and perhaps beyond the boundaries of this country, because the nations of the world are watching how democracies conduct themselves today, that we are not dealing fairly with redistribution. When you touch the basis of representation the ordinary elector feels somewhat shaky and jittery, particularly when he finds that there is a majority in the House of Commons who can perhaps change the constituency in which he is in such a way that he will not be able to have the same type of representation that he has previously enjoyed. This means that there is a heavy discretion, if I may say so, and with it a heavy responsibility resting upon the Prime Minister and the government in connection with the matter.
I do not ask the Prime Minister to do unreasonable things. If I am asking anything unreasonable please refuse it, because I do not want anything unreasonable with respect to this or any other matter. I do not think
the Prime Minister will believe that it is unreasonable. In the case of the constituency of the hon. member for Lake Centre, what a very simple matter it would be, without affecting anybody seriously, to remove the three townships at the top of his constituency of which he has spoken, which I fancy might be described by a former minister of agriculture, as he described a similar jutting out in his constituency in 1933, when he called it a wart, and which was referred to by the hon. member for Lake Centre as a knob. It would be so simple an operation that you would not have to give the patient a general anaesthetic. All he would need would be a local one. It would not require any major operation, and it would meet what the public conscience of Canada would require in a case such as this. The Prime Minister would have such a response across Canada that he would feel satisfied with it. It would remove a great deal of the difficulty which will normally attend discussions from now on after this bill has been passed, if the government and the Prime Minister particularly would bow to that very small request, but one, Mr. Chairman, which I think can be made with every good reason and which has a good foundation for it. I appeal to the Prime Minister as I have never appealed to him before to see if he will, before the schedules to the bill are reached, give consideration to that change and to see if we cannot get through this session with the public saying, well, at last in Ottawa they are trying to do a reasonable job; they are trying to be fair to political friends and opponents as well. When the schedule is reached I do not want to have to move an amendment incorporating what I have said. I shall be very much disappointed if I have to do that. I make this appeal to the Prime Minister in a way, as I said before, that I have never done before in the House of Commons because I feel keenly and deeply that this is something that should be remedied, not just in the interests of the hon. member for Lake Centre, but in the interests of a better public conscience and a better system of democracy in Canada.

Section agreed to.

It has been suggested in the press and in the house that the Ontario subcommittee did not make nearly as many changes as the circumstances warrant and there may be some justification for this view. However, it should be remembered that all the evidence before the subcommittee showed that there had been a substantial increase in the 
population of Ontario since 1941 and it was strongly urged in the committee that no changes of any kind should be made in view of this and having in mind that the next census is only 4 years hence. Nevertheless, this was not considered to be sufficient reason for postponing those changes which were equitable and unlikely to be affected materially by the census of 1951. In the end, the committee report was unanimous except for one constituency.
As to the changes, it will be sufficient to point out that the most obvious problem which had to be solved was that created by the large populations in the northern constituencies. The people of northern Ontario have been underrepresented for some years-at least as far 'back as the 1933 act when the constituency of Nipissing had over 88.00(1 people and was the largest in numbers in Canada returning one member. The committee of that year reduced the western Ontario membership by three and probably felt that they could not take another seat to provide two for Nipissing. But wffien the 1941 census showed that this 88,000 had grown to
113,000	and that Nipissing. Cochrane and Timis-kaming together had over 246,000 people, it became necessary to provide for five instead of three members. It will be seen that Central Ontario has the lowest unit of representation and the subcommittee considered it in order to reduce the membership by one. This was done by combining the districts of Parry Sound and Muskoka and by transferring the towmships of Rama. Mara, Thora and Brock to the constituency of Victoria and by transferring the townships of Scott and Uxbridge to the constituency of Ontario. 'This decision v'as made after careful study of other possible combinations in Central Ontario-there are at least 3 obvious alternatives.
The people in Parry Sound and Muskoka districts are the best of neighbours and have a great deal in common. I do not wish to delay the committee longer. I assure the committee that no effort was made to lose the services of the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario. So far as this party is concerned, we are most happy to have him continue as president of the dominion Progressive Conservative association. I feel that perhaps, after yesterday, we might hope that he would retain that office for a long time. But that is only by the way.
All these figures I have given indicate to the committee, I hope, that northern Ontario had to have not only the one seat allowed by the bill but another. They indicate that there was only one section of Ontario from which
it could come, namely, central Ontario. Other alternatives were considered, but none of them were as acceptable as this and none of them were as acceptable to the committee as a whole which represented Ontario, for this reason-and I will reduce the discussion, if I may, to a political level. Any other decision that we might have made would have eliminated one Conservative seat, by throwing two of them together. As it is now, we leave my hon. friend thrown in with a Liberal and with almost even chances of reelection. I think he will find that is so and I know he has sludied the figures.

I really feel flattered considering how little objection has been taken to the redistribution of the Ontario seats. That is the same thing as occurred last time. The schedules went through rapidly. The discussion which has gone on here pertaining to the other provinces just gives us an idea of what we are up against and is a basis for the argument that I have used for many years in this house, namely, that the time has come when redistribution should be performed by a commission consisting perhaps of the surveyor general, the chief statistician, the chief geographer, and other officials of the country. One can picture what will happen next time. In Ontario the advice I gave when the bill was introduced, namely, to let the ridings remain very largely as they are because within five years we shall have another census and another redistribution, was largely followed. I cannot see it at all, because nothing could have been gained by changing it.
At the next redistribution, what are we going to be up against? Ottawa should have another seat. Everybody knows that. Toronto will have to have at least two more seats. We all know that.

Welland has to have another seat. At the next election Welland will have about 100,000 population more or less. The province of Ontario must make up its mind to provide six seats from somewhere, and they may have to come off rural ridings. For that reason I do not want to be on the next redistribution committee, if redistribution is done by a parliamentary committee. It should be done by a commission, because this is what we are up against. We have made an exhibition of ourselves in the way we have been going on about these various seats.

The question will come all right, but this is important. We should not any longer bring this battle into the House of Commons and make an exhibition of ourselves to the people of the country. That is just about what this is; it is just an exhibition. I am not supporting everything that was done everywhere else, but I could defend anything that was done in the province of Ontario, even as to the seat which is represented by my good friend here, the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario. It is very comforting to find so few complaints in connection with the province of Quebec, and I think we owe thanks to the members of the subcommittee for the wonderful work they have done. I wish
also to thank the various members from that province for the help they have given in surmounting the various difficulties we encountered in adding eight new constituencies to that province, especially having in mind that this is the first time a number of new constituencies have been added there. This afternoon I was very much interested to hear the leader of the opposition commend this bill for having increased the number of members from the province of Quebec. Apparently he has changed his mind, because last year, when the redistribution bill was voted upon, he and all the members of his party voted against giving this increase to Quebec.

On a question of privilege, Mr. Chairman, I did not vote against Quebec having fair representation but against an amendment to the constitution which according to my lights was passed in an illegal way. I voted against that amendment, not against giving Quebec a fair quota, which I have always upheld. I made this clear in my remarks at that time.
The amendment would have had exactly the same result; that is, Quebec would not have had the eight additional members.

I rise to a question of privilege also. The hon. member has stated that we on this side voted against the measure on the ground that it aimed to correct an inequity in Quebec. That was not the basis of the objection at all, and the impression left by the remark of the hon. member is entirely false. I ask him to accept this statement, as I think everyone in the house will accept it. Certainly I never had any other view than that an inequity had been continued through the years. The government itself had made that decision at an earlier time, and I said this morning I neither criticized it nor condemned it. But I accepted the present decision and commended the government for making the correction, and I ask the hon. member to accept my statement.

I accept the statement of the hon. gentleman. The hon. member for Stanstead took the position in the subcommittee that he was representing all the opposition members, and made himself their advocate before the committee.
Yesterday the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario quoted Laurier in 1914, setting down some principles that should be followed in redistribution. He said the first principle was a substantial equalization of population; the second was the preservation of county units, and the third was justice to the electors. That is exactly the way we proceeded in the
Redistribution

Quebec subcommittee. First, we took the population of the province, according to the 1941 census, as 3,331,882, which is distributed in the various portions of the province mainly as follows: on the island of Montreal, 1,116,800; the city of Quebec, 156,640; the territory lying north of the St. Lawrence river, 934,547, and the territory lying south of the St. Lawrence, 1,123,888. These various districts, on the basis of the present representation, have the following average number of inhabitants per constituency: the island of Montreal, with its sixteen members, represented 69,800. The city of Quebec, with its three members, represented 52,215. The northern part of the province, with eighteen members, represented 49,186, and the southern portion with its twenty-eight members represented 41,625.
The members of the subcommittee felt that an average population of some 55,000 or
60.000	was more than adequate for urban constituencies, -whereas 40,000 should be the quotient for rural areas. Having agreed upon this principle, the committee decided that the representation of the island of Montreal should be increased, to such an extent as to reduce the 'population per constituency to the average already mentioned, that is, 55,000 to 60,000, and that the other districts should approximate as closely as possible the agreed quotients. The committee found that by adding to the population of the Island of Montreal that of Jesus island and increasing the representation by four the twenty new constituencies on the island of Montreal would average 56,921, the range being from
66.000	in thickly populated areas to 46,400 in semi-rural and sparsely populated districts. The addition to the city of Quebec of a suburb thereof increased the average for the said city to 53,620; and the addition of four constituencies to the northern part and one to the southern part practically equalized the two quotients at 41,304 for the northern part and 40,942 for the southern part.
Speaking of the northern part, the most populous constituencies were Pontiac, with 86,420; Chicoutimi, with 78,881; Charlevoix-Saguenay with 68,087 and Lac St. John-Roberval, with 64,306. The new constituency of Villeneuve was therefore created out of the northern portion of Pontiac, Lapointe out of the western half of Chicoutimi, and the other two were divided to become Charlevoix, Saguenay, Lac St. John and Roberval. In the southern district, after many small changes had been made the effect of which was to apportion more evenly the population of various constituencies, it appeared that the constituency of Gaspe was much too large, with its 57,588 inhabitants and 300 miles

of waterfront, exclusive of the Magdalen islands. The logical solution of the situation seemed to be a separate constituency for the islands. This decision is furthermore warranted by the fact that the islands lie 150 miles from Gaspe, to which they were heretofore attached, and 200 miles from Saguenay, and also by the lack of a proper transportation system from and to the mainland.
Yesterday the hon. member for Peace River attacked redistribution in the province of Quebec, though apparently from what he said he did not know what he was talking about, and said that all the constituencies represented by independent members had been touched, but no others. Those various constituencies in the province of Quebec which I have mentioned were not touched because they were represented by independents; it was because they were the largest in the province. I should like to place on Hansard the reactions of the various members, independent and others, when the committee report was tabled. I quote from Le Droit of April 23, 1947, as follows:
(Translation):
Mr. John Hackett, Conservative member for Stanstead, who acted as the representative of the Quebec independents on the redistribution committee, gave to understand, at the last meeting of the committee, on Tuesday, that most of his "proteges" seemed satisfied with their new legacy.
The independent member for Charlevoix-Saguenay, Mr. Frederic Dorion, whose constituency has been divided into two parts, has stated that the changes had been properly made in the Quebec district. On his part, Mr. Maxime Raymond, bloc populaire member for Beauhar-nois-Laprairie, does not appear greatly dissatisfied. As regards Mr. Georges Heon, independent Conservative member for Argenteuil, to whose constituency a large slice of Mr. Laeombe's has been added, we have been unable to ascertain his reaction.
The young and fiery Social Credit member for Pontiac, Mr. Real Caouette, told us calmly, during a brief interview in the lobby of the House of Commons, while puffing at a fragrant cigar, that he had every reason to be satisfied with the changes made in his constituency.
He said:	"The committee left me the part
of my constituency which is the best both from the Social Credit and the industrial standpoints. I took my largest majority in that area. On the other hand, they have taken away the older Pontiac, where the people are equally divided between Liberals and Conservatives. I can assure you that Villeneuve-the name of Mr. Caouette's new constituency-will vote Social Credit at the next election. The division of my constituency was a necessity in the interests of the province. Besides, by 1951, that district will probably have a third constituency, because the population has increased twofold since the last census was taken, seven years ago, and it is steadily growing. To my mind, redistribution was quite fairly carried out in the whole province of Quebec."

There you have the way in which the report impressed various independents in the house.
Before dealing particularly with the three constituencies which have been mentioned, I should like to place a tabulation on Hansard as a reply to what the hon. member for Lake Centre said this morning with regard to minority representation. It is interesting to note that in the present parliament minority representation is on the opposite side of the house rather than on this side. There were 63-1 per cent of the members of the cabinet elected by a clear majority. In the case of Little Chicago 57-5 per cent of the members were elected by a clear majority. On this side of the house 48 per cent of the members, or 61 out of 127, had clear majorities. If we look on the other side we find that. 27 out of 68, or 39-7 per cent of the Conservatives, wore elected with a clear majority. In the C.C.F. there were only three out of 28, or 10-7 per cent, and in the Social Credit group there was only one out of 14, or seven per cent. The members who were elected' by a clear majority number 61 on this side and 31 on the other side. I thought those figures would be interesting to the committee.
I do not think I need to deal particularly with Wright-Gatineau because the committee has already dealt with that. The constituency of Pontiac before redistribution had 86,000 population. It was first suggested that that constituency should be split in two. I thought myself that it would be preferable to divide it into three, taking the mining section on the north, the rural section in the centre, and the rural-English speaking section in the south. However, it was found that the southern portion had a population of only 49,000. After due consideration, it was decided that that was not a sufficient population to create a new constituency, particularly in view of the fact that the other two constituencies which would be created in the same area would have populations below 30,000. After consultation with the hon. member for Pontiac and others, it was agreed that the best solution would be to cut the constituency in two.
I have in my hand a resolution from the citizens of the town of Temiskaming asking that they be included in the southern part of the country, I have also other resolutions telegrams and letters asking that the provincial constituency of Temiscaming be not split in two. I have also telegrams from the chamber of commerce and from the prefect of the county of Temiskaming asking that they be joined with the southern portion of the con-83166-362

66,000.	The present division is something like

I am amazed at this amendment at this stage of the session. We appointed a committee which went thoroughly into this matter. speechtext: They have that now.

No, with all due respect for' the Minister of Veterans Affairs. The county of Halifax geographically covers a much larger area than the city of Halifax and includes farmers, fishermen and lumbermen, and when an -election takes place in that city on the dual member basis the people in the county have not the opportunity of nominating anyone -to contest the seat who would adequately represent the outlying sections of the riding and know something of the problems of the people -there. In addition to that, when an election is -held, the city of Halifax makes the nomination, and with all due respect to the men they send here they are not, in my opinion, sufficiently familiar with the problems of the farmers, fishermen and lumbermen in -that large area of the constituency lying outside the city to ,be able -to present their problems. Halifax has two representatives representing the city, professional men who when the session is over go back to their own business and seldom see the people in -the outlying sections. As a result, the people in the outlying sections have not the representation in this house which they should have. I

Redistribution
am absolutely opposed to this amendment, because what it is doing is this. It is harnessing that whole community to machine politics in the city of Halifax.
I am not concerned with who is elected, so long as the people of Halifax are given a fair opportunity to select their candidate from their own community, not a candidate in a law office 150 miles away, when the majority along that coast are fishermen, farmers and lumbermen. Under this dual member system they are not given a chance to exercise that democracy for which we are supposed to stand. The chief electoral officer, Mr. Castonguay, in the evidence I read before the committee, was strongly in favour of splitting .this riding in two and giving both the city and the rural community an opportunity of making their own selections. speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I want to explain this
matter to the committee as I understand it. From confederation down to the present time the city of Halifax has been a dual con-

stituency. Every party makes a practice of nominating one Catholic and one Protestant candidate. It is one of the traditions that may be good or bad in the province of Nova Scotia, we live in a considerable degree of amity as between the members of the various religious denominations, but we do that only by being careful to respect these long standing traditions.
It was felt early this session that the time had come when perhaps a clean sweep could be made of this practice of having dual constituencies in .the Dominion of Canada There were only two left at that time; the city and county of Halifax was one, and Queens county, Prince Edward Island, was the other. My own feeling was that it would be desirable, if possible, to get rid of dual member constituencies everywhere. The committee started out with that in mind. There were no representations to the contrary from anyone in Halifax so far as I could ascertain. As the committee continued on with its business, difficulties developed in Prince Edward Island, and the committee decided that they would, for reasons which I know nothing about, but which apparently commended themselves to the committee, leave the county of Queens, Prince Edward Island, a dual constituency. The committee was then in this position, that they would be wiping out the dual constituency probably everywhere except in Queens county, Prince Edward Island. At about that stage, certainly after the committee brought in its report, these representations came. I cannot tell the names of the persons, but it was reported to me that strong representations were made to the effect that the eighty-year long standing arrangements, one Catholic and one Protestant candidate for the parties, should continue.

I can see how it is. I think if you will check back on the St. Xavier's extension movement you will see that that is how it happened. These people have broken down the difficulties between Catholics and Protestants, and you find these people now working together in every organization for the purpose of trying to advance these organizations.
Even if the situation were as the minister suggests, I do not see how you would be disturbing the allocation. If there were a religious basis to what the minister says I would be one of the first members of the house to say, leave it alone, particularly if there were a danger of disrupting the community from a religious point of view. I do not think there is. For example, in Halifax, if the population of that city warrants the nomination of someone of the Presbyterian faith or of some other faith that is not Catholic, it is their privilege to nominate someone of that faith in the city. On the other hand, if in the other section of the community the Catholic faith is dominant and they desire to maintain that position by nominating someone of that faith, it is the business of the people of the community to make their nomination accordingly. If you go through most of the ridings in Canada, and particularly through the maritime provinces, where there are single member ridings, you will find that care is taken to see that traditions of the past are maintained on that basis. There is no reason in the world why this division cannot be made here and the nomination be made according to the dominant religions in the two ends of the constituency.
Travelling through that riding during the election, I came to the conclusion that two members from the city of Halifax cannot adequately represent that riding. It is scattered; it is hard to get around; it requires a lot of

travelling. There are diversified interests with which a member should be familiar. I believe that the coastline, which is predominantly fishing, some farming and a little lumbering, should have a member selected from these communities, so that he may be available to advise and counsel them on their problems which dovetail into the realm of government.
I am completely opposed to this business. I respect the minister's opinion and I have some idea of what it means, but I do not think the dividing of that area so as to permit those whose interests are not similar to select representatives suitable to themselves can be objected to. It would be in the best interests both of the member and of the community, and I do not believe that the minister's fears have any grounds so far as religion is concerned. This has been a debate which may cause a good many people in the country to despise this parliament and thus undermine this institution, and that is a bad thing at this time. It does seem to me that members of parliament have been forced into the position of looking after their own interests, and that does not go well with the people of the country.
With regard to the Halifax seat, I should like to know. what the technique was in securing changes in a committee report brought to the house. Who are the people who made representations-persons unnamed-sufficiently strong to override the will of a parliamentary
committee? I should like to know who they are. I will tell you what I believe, Mr. Chairman, if I may do so. I happened to be in Halifax for two or three days at the end of last week and I know something of what the pre-election canvass was both in Halifax and in the surrounding territory. My belief is that the Liberal canvassers in their reports indicated that, if this city were split, the government on another occasion could not carry the rural side of the riding, and that is where the representations came from.
That is another example of the kind of political gerrymandering we should have avoided. Our party moved a motion in February that this question should be decided by an independent commission. The Prime Minister was in accord with that motion, and I counted nineteen members of the Progressive Conservative party who voted for it. But it looked to me as though, in spite of what the Prime Minister's private opinion might be, the Liberal majority had come to the conclusion that they would' not permit that to be done because they were in power, and consequently there was a solid vote on that side of the house against the proposal.
The Prime Minister is a gentleman who is respected generally in the house. We look upon him as having had some influence in the growth and development of the Liberal party; and I regret exceedingly that, holding the view he did and expressing it, he was not able to set an example to the Liberal majority by trying to dio something to remove from this house the kind of controversy we have had during the last few days.
I think today's debate has -been a scandalous one. I want to support the member for Cape Breton South, because I believe that what he says is absolutely correct, that the city man with the professional or business point of view, representing the city constituency, cannot adequately represent the rural part of the riding. Rural problems of lumbering, fishing and farming are entirely different from the problems in a city. I have always felt that a member of parliament who sits for a riding where the economic interests of the people are identical is in a much better position than one who sits for a mixed riding. I have felt that in dealing with the problems of my own constituency. Because I represent a rural and farming community, I was, particularly before I became leader of this party, able to give more attention to these problems than to any other problems in the house. The committee recommended the division of the Halifax seat and I think it should be carried through.
With regard to the religious angle, I agree with the hon. member for Cape Breton South.

I know how important it is to many people that certain persons of certain religious persuasions should represent certain constituencies, and I sympathize with that point of view. But I Believe that the problems we face today in this parliament, seeing that we do not deal with education, and the cultural aspect of education, are largely economic and political. It seems to me that the argument which has been advanced on the other side in that regard is not sufficiently impressive to justify the change that is now proposed. I was going to say that it is not necessary to approach this matter from a political point of view. It is my view, though hon. members may differ, that no member of this house has a monopoly on the seat which he for the moment holds. I think the people back home are the ones who will make the final redistribution when election time comes around. We in this house should strive to make the constituencies conform as closely as possible to the wishes of the people. I realize that there are difficulties and that representation on the basis of population alone cannot be achieved in our country. However we should

Redistribution
try to come as close as we can to attaining that objective, taking into consideration the size of the constituency, the density of the population-and I am speaking of quantity -and the number of cities or towns which happen to be in a certain area.
The situation to which I refer is this. The new constituency of Portage la Prairie-Neepawa, or Portage-Neepawa as it is referred to here-is smaller in population than Dauphin, according to the schedule. In my opinion, that should be the other way round, for this reason. For one thing, the constituency of Portage-Neepawa is far more accessible, so far as roads and railways are concerned, than is the constituency of Dauphin. Second, there are three fairly large towns in that area, namely, Neepawa, Portage la Prairie and. 'Carberry, while in Dauphin there is only one town of any size, namely the town of Dauphin. Taking it on that basis, I would have expected that the committee would arrive at the conclusion that if there ought to be a larger population in one constituency than in the other, it should be in Neepawa-Portage rather than in Dauphin. I am saying this from a practical point of view. I am quite certain, incidentally, that all members, prospective members or candidates in the Dauphin area will agree with me on that basis, that adding any more to Dauphin, taking into consideration its size, the condition of the roads and so on, is not doing justice to the Dauphin constituency.
A little while ago I mentioned that the leader of the opposition had complained that his constituency was being amalgamated with another one, in which process a seat would be lost. My amendment which would restore Dauphin to its original boundaries and give back to Neepawa the two rows of townships which have been offered to Dauphin, would be one step toward restoring the constituency of Neepawa. If the other members would be willing to give up what they have taken away, then Neepawa would1 be restored to its original boundaries. However, on any basis you want to look at it, that of population or any other, I believe there is no argument that Dauphin should be given this piece of territory which might be referred1 to as a knob, as the hon. member for Lake Centre described it in his own case. It does not fit into the Dauphin constituency on the basis of community interest, as was argued by the chairman of the Manitoba committee. I have done some investigating on that score, and I find that the people in that part of the Neepawa constituency which has been added to Dauphin, which includes the towns of McCreary and LaurieT, do not do their business in the town of Dauphin. I have lived in that area all my
life, and I think I know what I am talking about. They do a certain amount of business in Neepawa and they take trips to Winnipeg, which lead them right through the cities of Neepawa and Portage la Prairie.
Another good reason why that area should not be added to Dauphin is that the eastern portion of it, that which lies along the shore of lake Manitoba, is connected by railroad to the city of Portage la Prairie. It is a branch line which runs from the city of Portage la Prairie. It is not connected by railroad in any direct way with the town of Dauphin. It is true that there is a road through to the town of McCreary, which road is only accessible during certain parts of the year. If someone were to take a trip by train from the town of Alonsa, which is near lake Manitoba, and was going to see his member of parliament in Dauphin, he would have to go to Portage la Prairie on a branch line where the train runs only three times a week, I understand, wait at Portage la Prairie for the next train, and go all the way back to Dauphin. Then he would have to come back by the same route. It would take two or three days to make the trip. My point is that it is not a sensible arrangement, and I am sure that hon. members, who have studied the map will realize that. It is for these reasons that I wish to suggest an amendment. The hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard agreed unanimously with that report and then put the proviso in, "with the exception of Kamloops". The representative of the C.C.F. party will bear me out that I am correct in that statement.
We have heard the discussion about Van-couver-Quadra. They are adding names with which I am not familiar. I happened to be drawn into this because originally I was on the committee. At the suggestion of some hon. members I withdrew my name because my riding was not interfered with. Because I was not familiar with the ridings in Vancouver which were to be altered, I was glad to get out

of the extra work. When I hear the hon. member for Vancouver South taking up a lot of time in discussing my colleague, the hon. member for Vancouver North, and talk about Quadra and about the hon. member for Vancouver East-who is going to be hard to beat, I admit, but we have hopes even of beating him-and talk about other ridings I want to say this about Cariboo. There was absolutely no intention to interfere with that riding in a political way. We have interfered to this extent. We have interfered with it in the way which was mentioned by the minister who represents British Columbia in the house when he spoke about the Yukon. Everybody in British Columbia is entitled to representation. We did not think it would be possible for the hon. member for Cariboo to give full representation to that riding, no matter how capable he might be. The immensity of the area is such that it is impossible for one man to represent it properly. Therefore we thought a portion of it should be added to Kamloops. For that reason we suggested that a certain portion of Cariboo be taken into the Kamloops riding. I have yet to hear any complaint from any organization or any individual, either in Kamloops or in Cariboo, that this was done for political reasons.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Order. We have an amendment to this schedule. Moved by Mr. Green:
That the 'bill be amended by deleting from the schedule thereto under the heading of British Columbia all reference to the ridings of Cariboo, Fraser Valley and Kamloops, and substituting therefor the description of the said ridings as contained in the schedule to the Representation Act of 1933.

Mr. Chairman, perhaps when I spoke yesterday I was in error in saying that I thought my friend, the hon. member for Fraser Valley, would have been more fair if he had been representing the government on this redistribution committee.
Nobody could have been more fair than I would have been.

After listening to his speech this evening, I feel that perhaps he is not quite so pure and innocent as I thought he was yesterday. However, the fact remains that I have nothing to retract of my statement yesterday in regard to the proposed change in the Kamloops riding, and the amendment which has been moved is for the purpose of leaving the boundaries of the riding as they are at the present time. That also, of course involves leaving Fraser Valley and Cariboo as they are at the present time. The Kamloops riding is already a huge riding. It took the sitting member over five

Redistribution
weeks last summer to get around to the main points in the riding and he was not going by street-ear either.
He must have been crawling on his hands and knees.

He was going by motor car. The hon. member for Fraser Valley has said that it is the smallest riding in. population in British Columbia. He is not correct in that statement. There are four small ridings in British Columbia all with a population in 1941 of under 33,000. Kootenay East, 25,559; Kamloops, 27,387, Skeena, 29,612, and Cariboo, 33,002. The proposal is to take about 8,000 people from the Cariboo riding, which would reduce it to 25,000 and add them to Kamloops, which would make it 35,000. That shows pretty well what is being done. On the other hand, the riding which adjoins to the south, that of Yale, has a population of 51,874. That is where the extra population should have come from to bring up the Kamloops riding, not only because Yale is so much larger than Cariboo, but also because the interests of the people of Kamloops are more closely akin to those of the people of Yale than of Cariboo. The part that has been added) now lies over a ridge of mountains. It is served by an entirely different railway, the Pacific Great Eastern, which is a British Columbia government railway; the city from which that new area gets its supplies, and with which it is most frequently in contact, is the city of Vancouver and: not the Kamloops district at all. The change is not a fair one.
Furthermore, there will be a redistribution again in 1951. British Columbia, at the present rate of growth of population, will then be entitled to several additional members, one or more of whom will have to be fitted into the interior of the province. It is likely that all the interior ridings will have to be changed and I suggest that it is unwise to make this change at the present time for a period of three or four years.
The real problem in the Cariboo is the fact that a portion of it, the Peace River district, is detached from the rest and one has to get to that district by plane from Prince George. This change now proposed does not help that situation. The change is, I believe, made for political purposes.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Oh, no.

I say that, believing it to
be true. I do not make such statements if I do not believe them. The Liberals had a majority of 500 in this district that has been added to Kamloops, and the C.C.F. also had a majority over the Conservative. The Kamloops fight was a very close one.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
May I say publicly
to my hon. friend what I said privately to him, that as one in charge of federal Liberal activities in British Columbia I never took the slightest part in any interference with the boundaries of any constituency.

I am not blaming the
Minister of Veterans Affairs, but I say again that this change is made for political purposes, and I know that is done. We need not try to shut our eyes to what goes on. It was made for that purpose, because the member for Kamloops got in by a small majority and this difference of 500 is more than enough to defeat him.
That sort of thing should not, I submit, be countenanced. It is most unfortunate to make an attack of this kind on a young member such as the hon. member for Kamloops, who has made such a splendid start in a public career. The hon. member for Fraser Valley has done a good job in trying to defend a bad job done by his good friends, but, no matter what he may say, I do not believe the people of my province appreciate an action of this kind, and I believe they will swing in and support the hon. member for Kamloops just because there has been this attempt to put him out of public life.

I do not know
whether the member for Kamloops has spoken on this question. I enjoy hearing him at any time, and we hear him frequently in this house. But does the hon, member for Vancouver South say that at any time I suggested that this portion of my riding be taken out of my riding and put in the Kamloops riding?
One town is taken out of the riding of the hon. member for Fraser Valley in order to -make a straight line across the southern part.
Would that not be good business?

A small Tory majority was got rid of when it was taken out. There is the picture. I would appeal to the Prime Minister and submit to him that this is an unfair move and one that should not be allowed to go through. I suggest that the riding be left as it has been since 1933. Actually, with the growth in population since that time, according -to the ration book figures, there are practically as many people in Kamloops as in the Cariboo riding and it has been growing quickly. I move -the amendment.

I think I ought to say a few words on the amendment. I am going to oppose it. I hope the committee will believe me when I say that personally I am
Redistribution

not very much interested where ,the line runs, but I think, in fairness to the committee for British Columbia and to the main committee, I ought to make this point clear. In my opinion the change that has been proposed for the Cariboo riding is very fair indeed. I need hardly tell the committee that the two ridings of Skeena and Cariboo comprise nearly two-thirds of British Columbia. I need not tell hon. members that it is not possible for any man, in the period between sessions, to cover those ridings. It has been said that someone spent five weeks in the attempt. I spent every day from the closing of the house until Christmas eve and did not cover one-third of it, and it cost me $1,700 to do that.
The committee's job was to put two new ridings into British Columbia and to arrange the boundaries of the ridings in such a way as to be fair, having regard to population and having regard also, I presume, to territory. The fact of the matter is that the Cariboo and Skeena ridings are at the north part of British Columbia and join each other, and Skeena joins up on the other side with Comox-Albami, which is another very large riding. There was no way of taking any part from either Cariboo or Skeena except the way in which it was done. They could not take anything off Skeena and give it to Comox-Alberni because that ds big enough now. They could not take anything off Skeena and give it to Cariboo because Cariboo is big enough now. They could not take any portion off north Cariboo because that goes up to the Northwest Territories. They could not 'take any off the east side because that touches Alberta. Therefore the only place they could take any part off to equalize the situation was to take some part of the southern end of Cariboo riding.
I ask the committee whether what was done was fair and impartial, and I say that it is both fair and impartial. It has already been stated that the population of Kamloops was 27,387. Cariboo was 33,000, and I point out that in the north country, and especially along Prince George, the population has increased very rapidly in the last two or three years. I would not be surprised if it were a third more than it was at the last election.
I wish to compare the population of the rural ridings of British Columbia as they now stand under the measure as it is proposed. Kootenay East for instance, is 25,559; the new Cariboo will have 26,396; Skeena will have 29,612; new Kamloops will have 33,993, and so on. So that if you take all the rural ridings and all the semi-rural ridings in British Columbia, you will find that Kamloops has not been unduly harshly dealt with in so far as numbers are concerned; and in so far as 
territory is concerned, Kamloops is still a small riding compared with either Skeena or Cariboo. Further, I think anyone who knows the territory well will admit that the southern part of the riding which it has been proposed to put into the Kamloops riding is easily worked from the Kamloops end, and it seems to me to impose no difficulty on anybody.
I want to add just one thing more. I have great admiration for the hon. member who sits for Kamloops constituency, as I have for a great number of other young men whom I see in parliament today, in all parties in this house. I hope they will keep on coming back to parliament as long as they have something in their upper stories; and I think the hon. gentleman to whom I have referred has something there. I hope he will come back. To think that anybody would go out of his way to impose such a situation in order to keep a young man out of the house, to me seems absolutely ridiculous. I cannot imagine that either the Liberal party or any other party would stoop to such a thing as that. When I examine the facts, I really find no grounds whatever for any such accusation.
Mr. MacNICO'L: I want to say a word about this amendment, knowing the area fairly well. The riding of Kamloops and the riding of Cariboo on the last occasion-and that was in 1933-were laid out so that one riding would embrace the watershed of the Thompson river; that is, the riding of Kamloops embraces the watershed of the North Thompson and the South Thompson river and the riding of Cariboo embraces the watershed of the Fraser river. To my mind, that was the sensible way in which to lay out those two ridings with a range of mountains between them. But the way in which those ridings are now laid out according to the changes now being made, appears to me to be a violation of the principles which should guide any committee in laying out ridings. At present, in the case of Cariboo, it is in one watershed west of a range of mountains, and in the case of Kamloops it is in another watershed east of a range of mountains.
I have a good deal of sympathy with the hon. member who represents Cariboo because at the moment, as he says, he has to take a circuitous route to go from one part of his riding in order to get to the part in northeastern British Columbia which is east of the mountains up in the Fort St. John area. There are, I believe, four centres there, namely, Rolla, Pouce Coupe, Fort St. John and Dawson Creek, and one might include Hudson Hope. It does not take very long to go there, and at the moment the British Columbia gov-

Redistribution
ernment is driving a road through Pine pass which will connect all the roadways in British Columbia west of the mountains with the roadways in the northeast part of the riding of Cariboo. I would think it would only have been common sense to allow those ridings to remain as they were until the next redistribution five years hence; because, as the hon. member for Vancouver South said, British Columbia has already increased its population since 1941 sufficiently to warrant its having another two members. It is growing so rapidly that by 1951 it will likely have the right to another four members. I am glad to see British Columbia growing like that. They now have eighteen members. I presume that, after the next redistribution, they will have twenty-two members of parliament, and then all these little things can be ironed out. Why make all this change now? When the house commenced considering this question, I tried to induce it to let things stay largely as they were until the next redistribution, when the whole thing could perhaps be ironed out by a commission which will do the thing properly.

I want to say just one word on this, inasmuch as I was the representative of this party on the redistribution committee. I should like to say that the territory which has been taken from Cariboo and attached to Kamloops geographically and economically has all in common with Kamloops. It is a cattle and sheep country.
What about the mining area at Bridge river?

The mining area at Bridge river is just a little spot on the map which breaks the general rule. You will find that situation anywhere. I have a mining camp sitting up on the Portland canal all by its lonesome. You cannot eliminate that. But that area, taken in general, has all in common with Kamloops riding. And when redistribution takes place again, it is doubtful whether that territory will be upset inasmuch as it has that economic affinity.
It has a lot of sheep, anyway.
The hon. member for Vancouver South has attacked the hon. member for Vancouver North, saying that he had done this with political ends in view.
I must ask for that statement to be withdrawn.
What is the hon. member saying?
That is what the hon. member said.

speechtext: Yes. My hon. friend used the words "political motives". I am sorry to have to remind him of that.
No. The hon. member for Skeena said that I had political motives in view when I made that statement.
No, no.

speechtext: He said that you accused others. If my hon. friend will pardon me for reminding him of it, he did say that these changes were made with political motives.
I thought be was saying that I had political motives in raising this question.

speechtext: No.

I do not imagine that the hon. member for Vancouver North is an absolute innocent as far as dealing with his own political party is concerned. But I will say that on this committee he was frank and in the open, and we knew what the score was, right along the line. In the sittings of the committee we got along well until the hon. member for Vancouver South came back and we made adjustments because of his demands. If I had known this was coming up later, I would never have agreed to them; but just to keep peace in the family I did.
The hon. member will know better next time.
Blessed1 are the peacemakers.

What I cannot understand about these representatives is this. They get up and make appeals for this individual and that individual. I am not now speaking in a detrimental fashion having regard to the hon. member for Kamloops. But one would think some of these people were ordained by the Lord to represent the people.
In their own estimation.

I think it was Bernard Shaw who said that Great Britain had plenty of brains, but they were all in the gutter. It is the people of this country who must make up their minds who shall come to this house and who shall not, and it does not matter what province they come from. A great many pages of Hansard are being taken up by hon. members speaking and praying on behalf of an individual member; and that does not go down. As far as I am concerned, it is representation by the people for the people.

On the schedules-Saskatchewan.

I do not desire to make a speech; I expect to have considerable support for that statement, in any event. This afternoon I asked the Prime Minister if, before the schedules came up, he would consider some change, which I then delineated, with respect to the constituency of Lake Centre. I take it that the Prime Minister has decided against taking any steps in that regard', but I should like to leave the door open for him to do so, if I may; and in moving this amendment I would ask him, if possible, to give support to this change. I move:
That clause No. 4 on page 51 of the Saskatchewan section of the schedule to Bill No. 18 be amended by deleting from the electoral district of Lake Centre the following township, namely No. 82 in ranges 16, 17 and 18 inclusive both west of the second meridian, and adding the said township to the electoral district of Humboldt.

I wish to say a word on this amendment. As the bill stands at present, it gives Humboldt the largest population of any rural constituency in Saskatchewan, and by adding these townships from Lake Centre the difference between the population of those two constituencies will be made still greater. As I indicated this afternoon when I asked the hon. member for Lake Centre a question, I have many friends in the townships referred to, and they are not all of my political opinion. I believe there should foe a little balance in representation. I just want to say to those responsible for this bill that the amendment moved by the hon. member for Peel will not meet with any objection on my part. Whether these people be Liberals, Tories or members of the C.C.F., I shall be happy to have the opportunity of representing them. But on the argument presented to the effect that these townships belong geographically to Humboldt, and that they will foe better served if they are attached to that constituency, I would suggest that the hon. member for Lake Centre must be consistent and agree that township 32, ranges 21, 22, 23 and 24, which are closer to the town of Watrous, to which all communications lead and which town has 'been put into his constituency, should be added to Lake Centre. I think that would be only logical. I am not here to carry on any horse trading, but I submit that if it is logical to say that the townships enumerated by the hon. member for Peel should be in Humboldt, in spite of the fact that Humboldt already has a much larger population than Lake Centre, then it is also logical to say that those townships adjacent to the town of Watrous and Lake Centre should be taken into that constitu-
ency. Let me repeat, however, that I shall be happy to represent them, and if you want to add even a few more townships and) ranges I shall do my best.

I shall not detain the committee for more than a moment. I wish to say that if the hon. member for Lake Centre had not agreed to this proposition; if he had made it clear in the subcommittee as he and his leader have made it in the house that in order for him to get back to parliament it was important that he do not have these three extra townships, I certainly would have made an additional appeal and argued further with the hon. member for Melfort. But when the hon. member for Lake Centre agreed to this compromise proposal of mine when the hon. member for Melfort, by agreeing to it too, went halfway to meet him; when this proposal meant-and as matters now stand- Humboldt was increased to 4,500 above the average for rural seats, I thought I should not line up with the hon. member for Lake Centre in favour of the present proposition, as against the hon. member for Melfort who had already gone half way to meet him in agreeing to my compromise proposal. As far as I am concerned, I have no objection whatever to the hon. member getting rid of these townships. It was a matter of what seemed fair and just. It means nothing whatever to our party; it was only an endeavour to be fair, and I thought when the hon. member signed he was satisfied. If this amendment is carried it will mean that the population of Lake Centre will be reduced to 41,100, which will be 2,400 under the average. If the schedule goes through as it is, the population of Humboldt will be 48,000, 4,500 over the average; and if the amendment is carried, the population of Humboldt will be increased by another 1,800, which will make it 6,300 over the average for rural seats. That is the situation.
Amendment (Mr. Graydon) negatived: yeas, 24; nays, 75.

I should like to say a few
words, of protest in so far as the Weybum seat is concerned. I would not have said anything were it not for the fact that I have received a large number of telegrams and letters from residents and organizations of the city of Weyburn protesting vigorously over the elimination of the name "Weyburn" in the new seat which is to be set up in that area. The Weybum seat was set up in 1914 and has been known as Weyburn for thirty-three years. It is now being amalgamated with Wood Mountain, and the new seat is to be known as Assiniboia.

Criminal Code
This is rather confusing because the present seat of Assdniboia is and has been for forty years east of the city of Weyburn. Outside of the fact that it is confusing, it seems to me that this is great discrimination against the city of Weyburn. That city has been quite favourably known in Canada. It was the seat of the South Saskatchewan regiment and it is the most active and influential city in southern Saskatchewan. Several seats in the province carry the names of towns, such as Melfort, Kindersley and Rosthern, towns smaller than Weyburn. The name "Weyburn" means a lot to these people, both city and district, and they consider that it should receive better consideration.
I have a feeling of affection for the name "Assiniboia", because as a boy I was brought up in that area. I believe the name ought to be perpetuated, but I would draw the attention of the committee to the fact that it is being preserved in the town of Assiniboia, over 100 miles west of Weyburn. That is a thriving and progressive town bearing the name of the original territory and it does honour to that name. I do not think it is necessary to eliminate the Weyburn seat in so far as the name is concerned. I should have liked to see a hyphenated name with "Wey-bum" part of it. Since Wood Mountain is to be a part of the new seat, I would suggest Weyburn-Wood Mountain as an acceptable name.
I urge the committee to give this matter some consideration. We have a number of hyphenated names in Canada which are well known, and I would refer to Hastings-Peter-borough and other such constituencies. In fairness to the city of Weyburn, I should like to see the name of that city forming at least part of the name of the constituency being set up under the present redistribution.

maintopic: CASE OF J. G. ALLARDYCE-STATEMENT OF MR. HARKNESS

speechtext: Right Hon. IAN A. MACKENZIE (Minister of Veterans Affairs) moved that the house go into committee of supply.

maintopic: CASE OF J. G. ALLARDYCE-STATEMENT OF MR. HARKNESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the indulgence of the house to discuss briefly a matter which I have been requested to raise and which I shall have no other opportunity to bring before the house. I would not raise it at this late hour of the session if I did not think an important principle were at stake, the principle of under what circumstances and to what extent the Canadian government should protect Canadian citizens and their interests in foreign countries.
The case is that of John George Allardyce, a Canadian soldier who. served five years overseas. At the time he left for overseas he had a wife and son two years old. During the time he was overseas his wife became involved with a United States soldier stationed in Calgary, which is Allardyce's home town. 
When he returned from overseas he telephoned or wired from Halifax that he would arrive home at a certain time. The day before he arrived in Calgary his wife took the child and left for the United States. His information was that she was subsequently joined by the United States soldier. All his efforts to trace his wife and son proved abortive. He was particularly interested in getting back his son, who was then some seven years of age. The United States army would give no information as to the whereabouts of the soldier.
A short time ago Allardyce was served with a notice that divorce proceedings had been entered against him in the city of Seattle. Upon receiving this notice he took legal advice. He was in no position financially to go to Seattle to fight the divorce case, and if he had fought it, it would have done him no good so far as getting back his son was concerned. Therefore he or his solicitor wrote to the Department of External Affairs in Ottawa asking if they would request the United States government to take steps to have this man's son, who was a Canadian, of course, returned to Canada. The Department of External Affairs refused to take any action in the matter. This is a copy of the letter which they sent in reply:
I have received your letter of June 11, 1947, regarding this case. I regret to inform you that there is no ground on which the Canadian government could properly intervene with the United States government.
This is essentially a private civil dispute and, although we sympathize with Mr. Allardyce, I am afraid that his only recourse is to proceed in the appropriate court in the United States.
If Mrs. Allardyce had removed the child to another province of Canada or to another part of the British commonwealth, the position would be exactly the same. Mr. Allardyce would have to proceed in the courts in that place.
Even if the entry of the child into the United States were contrary to the immigration laws of the United States, that is not a matter about which , this government can complain. If the United States authorities do not choose to deport the child to Canada, we could not properly ask them to do so.
I am sorry that we cannot give you any helpful advice or encouragement, but the fact is that the government cannot properly intervene in private civil disputes.
Yours sincerely,
L. B. Pearson,
Under-Secretary of State for External Affairs
I have discussed this matter with the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. St. Laurent) ; and I must say that he appeared to me, to begin with, to be disturbed over this situation whereby a man who had served his country overseas and lost his son as a result of that service could be given no help to

J. G. Allardyce
regain custody of his son. It seems to me that the government has a responsibility in cases of this kind. If this man had been home in Canada he would have been able to protect his own interests; the case would have been an ordinary civil dispute, and there would possibly have been no question of the government's intervening on his behalf.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: CASE OF J. G. ALLARDYCE-STATEMENT OF MR. HARKNESS
speechtext: Where did this happen?

speechtext: At Calgary, Aliberta, while he was overseas serving in the army in defence of this country. In view of that fact, it seems to me that the dominion government has a responsibility to do its utmost to have the child returned to the father. speechtext: If I may interrupt, has this matter been taken up with the Department of Veterans Affairs?

maintopic: CASE OF J. G. ALLARDYCE-STATEMENT OF MR. HARKNESS
speechtext:
Not to my knowledge, unless it was taken up 'by Allardyce himself at the veterans affairs branch in Calgary. The course which he followed was to 'take it up with the Department of External Affairs, which deals with foreign countries.
There comes to my mind immediately the case which the Secretary of State for External Affairs brought up in the house two or three weeks ago, the case of the wife of Mr. Power, a Russian lady whom the Russian government refused1 to allow to come to Canada. I think the Department of External Affairs acted very properly in its efforts to get the Russian government to have that man's wife returned. But I think the case of this soldier who has lost his son really as a result of being overseas and not being home to protect his interests is an even stronger case, and one which there should be more reason for the Department of External Affairs to take up and attempt to have straightened out.
I do not want to take an undue amount of time on this case, but I should like to read one or two extracts from a letter which I received in connection with the matter, to show that there 'is strong feeling over it. This letter states:
There was a time when a Canadian who thought himself wronged in another country could invoke the aid of the British embassy and proper representations were made-no man was refused because of lack of wealth or prominence in life. The American embassies do not hesitate to assert the just claims of citizens of the United States. In Canada we have established our own diplomatic service which appears to have thrown over the British tradition in this respect without adopting the American. Surely our relations with the United States are not so unfriendly that representations on behalf of this man, who has served his country so faithfully in war, would be resented!
I think that is the case. I do not .think the United States government would resent for a moment representations made on behalf of a man who finds himself in this unfortunate situation.
The letter continues:
This young man is quite unable, financially, to go to Seattle to fight for the custody of his child in the courts there. Canada quite rightly refuses to adopt any system of easy divorce but is it not rather hypocritical for us to take this stand and at the same time facilitate an American soldier, who was stationed in Canada during the war, taking the child of a Canadian soldier who, because of service overseas, was unable to protect the child.
I should like to make a plea to the Secretary of State for External Affairs, to the government and to .the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Mackenzie) to interest themselves in this case, to make representations to the United States government to have this child returned .to its proper custodian who in this case, I am sure every hon. member will agree, is his father.
Right Hon. HAN A. MACKENZIE (Minister of Veterans Affaire): I wish to say just one word. I shall be glad .to cooperate in the fullest degree, but this is the first time I have heard a word about .this particular case. As soon as I got the particulars from my hon. friend, I shall be glad to discuss it with my colleague, the Secretary of State for External Affairs, to see what can be done.
Motion (Mr. Mackenzie) agreed to, and the house went into committee of supply, Mr. Macdonald (Brantford City) in the chair.
