I have a number of union men and labour men in my constituency, in spite of the fact that it is largely a farming area. Many of them are concerned with some of the operations of the Unemployment Insurance Act. I do not know that the minister can do anything about the main complaint which is that when a person becomes unemployed because of physical inability to carry out such duties as railroading he does not come under unemployment insurance. That is part of the act, is it not? Unless there was an amendment to the act I do not suppose that that could be changed.
That is correct.

But there is another feature to it, and I think there should be some way of getting around it. When a man becomes unemployed because there is no employment in his line of work and he cannot get a similar job he draws unemployment insurance. We will say that he draws it for two or three weeks at the appointed rate, and then he gets a cold or pneumonia and is confined to his bed. His wife goes down to draw the unemployment insurance; immediately he is considered unemployed because he is sick, and he cannot draw the unemployment insurance. Even though there is still no job, he actually loses his employment in the regular way under the act, but before he gets a new job he becomes ill, and then he is ill under the act and is unable to collect. Could not something be done about that situation?
Not without an amendment to the act. He has to be available for employment. That is the act.

I have a question which is along the same line. I understand that the Canadian Pacific railway and Canadian National railway shop men are pensionable at the age of sixty-five. I understand, too, that at that age, if they have not contributed to a pension fund they will get $30 a month. I wish the minister would say whether or not, if at that age they are receiving $30 a month pension and they are quite prepared to take on other employment and cannot obtain a job, will they still be able to take unemployment benefits?
That is the act and the regulations. Notwithstanding the fact they get superannuation at sixty-five, if they are fit and available for work they are entitled to unemployment insurance.
They would be entitled to it?

We have heard a good deal about War Assets Corporation. That being the case, I think it would be interesting for the committee and the country to know a little bit about the accounting of this corporation. I think it would also be interesting to know if there is any possibility of this corporation, as it were, going out of existence within the near future. I should also like to get some idea of the number of people in the employ of the corporation at the present time, and also whether the corporation as it now exists really justifies its existence.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Reconstruction and Supply):
speechtext: War Assets Corporation is still quite active. Up to the first of June its sales were running at a rate in excess of $10,000,000 a month, which is not small change in the view of this government. Sales in the month of June were, I believe, $7,300,000. It is likely that sales will continue at that level perhaps for the balance of the year.
What were the sales a year ago?
They were running about $20,000,000 to $25,000,000 a month. Total recovery to date is something in excess of $400,000,000, I beilieve; and a considerable volume of material remains to be disposed of.

What about the number of employees at 'the present time?

Supply-Reconstruction and Supply

Roughly, there are eight thousand employees. The number is dropping as we are able 'to close warehouses. As we can liquidate the contents of a warehouse now, the warehouse is closed and disposed of; and, of course, the men employed in the warehouse are dispensed with.
The numbers are dropping?
The numbers are dropping quite rapidly. The peak employment was something over 10,000. The staff .is dropping. The cost of sales is quite reasonable, running about thirteen per cent of the gross.

Has 'the minister ever put on record the amount of money which went into war equipment of all kinds during the war period? Has he ever given an estimate of how much was left when the war was over? Has he ever told the 'house how much of it has been declared surplus and thereby been made available for sale? Has he ever given a statement as to how much has been sold in each of the years since .the war has been over? Has he in mind the amount that is still available for possible future sale or other use? Those are a good many questions to ask at one time, but they ask for information which I think the country would like .to have. I suggest that, to the extent .the minister oan do so, he might try to get .that information before his estimates are finished.

It is difficult .to say what is the value of the material supplied to the Canadian army. I presume that is what my hon. friend is interested in. It will be recalled that in this country we made material which went to the British allies; it went to Australia; it went to the United States. Perhaps the Department of National Defence could give the value of the material which went to them, but the Department of Munitions and Supply would be unable to do so. They had material manufactured and delivered it as instructed. In some cases .the supply line to the Canadian troops would be a British supply line, as it was in Italy. In other cases it might be a Canadian supply line. The Department of Munitions and Supply would not have that information. The material was allocated by ihe munitions allocations committee. That committee was made up of the United Kingdom, the United States and Canada. Our production was placed before the committee, and it was allocated on the basis of need. If it was allocated to the United States, the United States paid for the material. If it was allocated to the United Kingdom, it was either paid for or charged to mutual aid. If it was 
allocated to Canada, .it was paid for by .the Canadian government. It is difficult to put a value on used material. If it was built for war, it was used for war and was returned here in such condition as it may have been in; or perhaps it never left Canada but was used for training purposes.
Aeroplanes are a case in point. An aeroplane may have cost $200,000 to build. It may be worth nothing for civilian purposes. For example, there is the Mosquito aircraft which cost, I think, something in excess of $200,000. There is no sale for it as a post-war aeroplane. There are a great number of them in store. Some fine day we shall take out the engines and all the parts which are worth salvaging, and destroy the rest. Aeroplane recovery is, I should think, in the vicinity of one or two per cent. In some materials it runs to perhaps sixty or seventy per cent, and in other materials it runs to 100 per cent. But there is no pattern of recovery in materials now. Whether it will be possible to obtain the figures which my hon. friend wants, I cannot say; but we shall certainly read this question in Hansard and submit the figures as best we can.
Another case in point is called to my attention by my officials, namely, that of the tank which cost $90,000 to build, when scrapped, it produces thirty tons of scrap which sells at $15 a ton. That is an indication of the salvage which can be expected from a war machine which has no peace-time value.

I believe the information I requested would be of great public interest, but I quite appreciate that the minister could not be expected to give the answers now. Can he say, through the use of figures or in any other way, what amount of this equipment already has been declared surplus; what are the revenues for each of the fiscal periods since the war, and any approximation of what amount the country will recover through what may yet be declared surplus and sold?

Supply-Reconstruction and Supply

It is difficult to forecast the further amount that may be declared surplus. The practice of War Assets Corporation is not to take account of any material that it has not in store. In other words, after the declaration is made we can assess the possibilities in regard to the material we have; but each month we obtain more material. We consider it fairly safe to say we expect to realize another 850,000,000, which would bring the grand total to well over $450,000,000.
That would be recoverable over the next year or two?
Yes; certainly over the next year.
Has the department ever made an estimate as to the percentage oi recovery, taking the original cost of this equipment and what the state derives from its sale?

We do not keep a record of original costs. It is too difficult to trace back and1 ascertain the original costs. I think we would have to give the estimate by categories. As I say in aeroplanes, which represent a very large part of the war expenditures, the recovery is almost nothing. Tanks are in the same category. However, from the war equipment which was surplus to the Canadian army when it stopped fighting we expect to recover some-think in excess of $450,000,000.

I have just one other observation, and perhaps the Minister of Finance would listen to this. It is possible that an accurate statement could not be obtained, but I suggest that it would be in the public interest to have an approximate statement of the amount of money the government of Canada put into what might be generally called war equipment; how much of that was wasted in war; how much was left when the fighting was over; how much has been declared surplus, and what the recovery has been. I gather from what the minister has said that there will be a recovery of around $450,000,000, but we have not even an approximate idea of the cost of the goods which will bring in that figure. I gather the minister has not even the approximate cost?
No.

I wish to make a few remarks on this item, if I am in order, with regard1 to housing; and to ask one or two questions concerning war assets. In my constituency we have a large number of veterans and others who are seeking homes, who at the present time are living in all sorts of accommodation, and in some cases, suffering a great deal of inconvenience. This situation existed
throughout the war, and it has not been improved since the end of the war. I believe the minister understands the particular difficulties that exist in my constituency, particularly in and around the city of Trail. Those difficulties are both legal and physical, because of the nature of the country and the limits of the city of Trail, and I do not believe they will be solved until we have a subsidized housing programme in which the dominion, the provinces and municipalities will cooperate.
That is all I am going to say in that connection, but I want to ask a question and offer a suggestion. Personally I believe it is all wrong that many of these veterans and other young people establishing homes in this country should be expected to assume mortgages covering a period of twenty years and amounting to $5,000, $6,000 and $7,000, in order to get homes. I believe we are doing a great deal too much of discounting the future which in the years that lie ahead may bring much grief to many families. I should like to ask the minister if any consideration has been given to partly building homes. What I have in mind is this. Instead of building a complete house and having it all ready to occupy, at a cost of from $5,000 to $7,000, perhaps the foundation could be put in and enough of the house built to serve temporarily as a habitation, with the idea that the purchaser would not assume an obligation of more than $2,000, and that he would complete the house at his leisure over a period of years. In many ways that would be a much sounder arrangement for many people who are trying to obtain 'houses and who must live on very modest salaries. That is the way in which a good many people established homes in this country in the early days, and I believe the government might well consider a scheme of that kind. Many young men desiring homes would be willing to undertake the building of houses on that basis, and would prefer to assume a total indebtedness of not more than $2,000 and then complete the house over a period of years in their spare time. At the same time they would 'be free of a great burden of debt. If something along this line could be done at this time we would save material; we would save labour, and we would certainly save the payment of a great deal of interest by many people desiring to establish homes. I believe that under this scheme it would also be possible to build more housing units in a given time. A scheme of this kind would apply perhaps more particularly outside the cities and towns. I should like the minister to say whether he has considered anything in that direction.

Supply-Reconstruction and Supply
My second question, is this. In my constituency are hundreds of houses formerly occupied by the Japanese, particularly at Slocan City, Lemon Creek and Roseberry. These houses are, on the average, fourteen feet wide and twenty-four feet long, and1 are quite well constructed. They would make excellent homes for many people, and in some cases if two of these houses were joined together they would make satisfactory quarters. A good many people in my riding would like to purchase these houses, and have been waiting two years for War Assets to dispose of them. I urge the minister to see that something is done to dispose of at least sufficient of these houses to meet the needs of those people living within perhaps twenty or thirty miles of where those houses are now located. They could arrange for their transportation by road or have them taken down and hauled1 to their small holdings or home-sites in the villages in my district. Can the minister give any information in this connection?

As far as partly completed houses are concerned, my hon. friend will appreciate that that will be an arrangement between the builder and the lending institutions. Loans under the National Housing Act are available for partly completed houses just as they are for fully completed houses. I am quite aware of the arrangement suggested by my hon. friend, and I realize that it is a thrifty method of building a house and one that should be taken advantage of more frequently. However, when the government builds, it builds to rent, and for that type of housing the units must be completed. As far as the houses at Slocan are concerned1, I am told that they are in the process of being declared surplus to War Assets Corporation. If that is the case, War Assets Corporation will immediately arrange for their disposal, and I have no doubt that local purchasers will be given consideration.

A few moments ago the minister mentioned the small amount received for tanks as scrap. I noticed a newspaper clipping some two or three weeks ago which stated that the defence department had purchased tanks from the United States government. Were those tanks different from the ones that are being sold at the present time?

For the sake of uniformity, some of the latest design tanks were bought by the armed services from the United States government, I think on the basis of a cent a pound or something like that. The purchase was on a scrap basis. These tanks are more

modern than the ones which were built in Canada in the early days of the war.
The minister mentioned Mosquitoes. I understand that in the United States they are spraying or cob-webbing their aeroplanes in order to preserve them. Is anything being done along that line here?

The air force are cob-webbing planes which they are keeping in store as active war planes, but planes declared surplus to War Assets are for disposal. There is no purpose in storing them. If the air force expected to need them, they would not declare them surplus.

What is the procedure when a sale is made by W'ar Assets? A sale is advertised in the paper to be held on such and such a date, and then they say, "subject to prior sale". A person arrives on the job thinking he is going to be able to buy something, but when he gets there he finds it is not for sale.

That seldom happens now. In the early days we had priority arrangements. The first priority went to government departments; the second priority went to provinces, and the third priority went to municipalities. If a sale was in process of being arranged and a priority claimant applied for the goods, the corporation had no option but to sell1 to the priority claimant, which meant that the goods would not be offered to the public. I am happy to say that we have now modified priorities. A sale may be subject to prior sale, but no prior sale takes place and the material1 is offered to the public.

I spoke to the Minister of Veterans Affairs, I think on May 2 or 3, with regard to some shrubs around the DVA hospital at Peterborough, and he advised me to get in touch with War Assets Corporation. I dropped them a line, but it was never answered. There was an advertisement in the Peterborough Examiner saying that the shrubs would be offered for sale, but when people went to pick them up they discovered there were two trucks from Toronto taking them all away.

We are not florists; we sell
war material. If my hon. friend wants to buy shrubs I strongly advise him to get them through a florist.
The Peterborough horticultural society wanted the shrubs to beautify the city, and it was a sore touch to them to have them carted off to Toronto.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I think I must assume some responsibility in support of my hon.

Supply-Reconstruction and Supply___
friend. He did come to see me about these. The hospital in Peterborough burned down.

The minister is not the
guilty party.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
When the hospital
burned down and it was not to be reassumed by us I think some adjustment might be made between the various agencies of goverm-ment and the city of Peterborough.

Some time ago I referred
to the crates that are in the Belleville yards. Some of those crates have 'been there for years, and new ones have been placed there within the last four or five months or even less than that. What is in them and why are they there?

That is a dump from which
we sell crated vehicles. The vehicles my hon. friend is talking about may have been sold and the buyer has not as yet taken them away. Every vehicle owned by War Assets has been sold.

They would not leave
them a year or two years.
They might.
They are pretty funny purchasers if they do that.

I understood the minister to say a few * I
moments ago that they had not been able to get costs.

We have not tried to get
costs.

Does that mean that you sell people things without knowing what they cost? There may be precious little realized on the original cost.
I should think it is blind business to sell things without having any idea of the cost. You have already indicated that in the case of aeroplanes and tanks you do know the cost, but do I understand correctly that you disregard costs entirely? Surely that is not so?

If it is an article which has
a ceiling price, we sell at the ceiling price. If the article has no common value, we have it valued. We follow a careful procedure on that. When material comes from the armed services we put a value on it and sell it, but that has nothing to do with the cost of manufacture.
Does that mean that there will be available anywhere even a rough computation of the original cost of these things that are being sold by the hundreds and millions?

We could trace down an
individual item if there was any interest. For example, we may sell a corvette which cost about $900,000 for about $90,000. I do not think the fact that it cost $900,000 would be of any particular interest to the buyer, to the seller or to anybody else.

It might be of considerable interest to the people of Canada to know the cost of these things which are being sold for hundreds of millions and which probably cost many times that. I am not criticizing that.
What kind of Canadian would find value in that information? What would he do with the information if he had it?
I think he would try to guess at whether there had been an efficient job done. We have no means whatever of guessing in the slightest degree at the efficiency of the performance.

A Mosquito aircraft which cost $200,000 may have been used in the war for a period and then be declared surplus to War Assets. The salvage value may be $5,000. Does that signify lack of efficiency on the part of War Assets?
I would not say so at all.
We may build a tank for $90,000 and sell it for $15 a ton. That does not show a lack of efficiency.
You do not have to convince me; I agree with that.
I am trying to get the hon. member to tell me what this bulk figure would do.

I appreciate that what you realize from the things you describe is the merest fraction of their cost. But what I am talking about is the large amount of more standard articles, which must have run into hundreds of millions of dollars, where you would know the cost and where people might form an estimate whether you were being efficient or not.

The difficulty is that the material we were selling was not confined to the last great war. We were selling 18-pounder guns from the first great war, and harness and saddles made for the South African war. The production of standard material was at a reasonable price. As more units got into operation and production speeded up, prices dropped, but we do not know when we are

Supply-Reconstruction and Supply
selling an article whether it was made in the early or late stages of the war, and I cannot imagine how, without an elaborate system, you could get that information.
Mr. MACDONN-ELL (Muskoka-Ontario): It need not be elaborate. From what the minister has said it seems to have been a free and easy performance. It would not have been much trouble to have got a pretty close approximation to the price; but, as it is now, there is a wide open escape for everybody.

A matter that has received wide attention is the disposal of the three plants at Trail, Welland and Calgary. I took this matter up in the house on the estimates of the Department of Agriculture, and I want to read briefly now from the Rural Co-operator of January 14, 1947, in connection with the disposal of these three plants which had been built during the war for production for war purposes and then, later, were converted to produce ammonium nitrate, a valuable ingredient in fertilizers. The article in the Rural Co-operator reads in part:
We reported last year respecting the disposal of the government-owned nitrate plants at Calgary and at Welland, Ontario. The situation at that time and throughout the year, so far as our understanding with the government was concerned, was that the government, through Hon. C. D. Howe, had assured us that, even though the Calgary plant, where cheap nitrate was being produced, might be sold, there would be protection for prices for nitrate for fertilizer through the fact that the government intended continuing operation of the plant at Welland.
Those of us who are connected with agriculture were most disappointed when we found that the government-and I say this frankly- had sold the Canadian farmer down the river in disposing of the plant to a United States concern whose only interest was to make profits in this country. We feel bitter about this. I should like to read from a letter that I received from the minister's own office dated March 24, 1947. I had written to the department in connection with the disposal of the Welland plant, and in reply I was informed that this plant was built at a cost of $19,129,246.02 to the Canadian taxpayer. The letter goes on:
On December 1, 1946, this plant exclusive of inventories was sold to North American Cyana-mid Limited for $4,750,000.
I do not think, by any stretch of the imagination, anyone could say that this was a fair price for the plant. I draw the attention of the minister to the fact that he did commit himself and the government to retaining one of these plants to produce a cheap fertilizer for the Canadian farmer. Second, I would

ask him to state why the Calgary plant was not kept in operation where, as has been stated, we could produce ammonium nitrate for about $19 a ton even before we got into post-war production, where with larger volume we could have reduced the price. I want to emphasize as strongly as I can that the government were urging an all-out production of food in this country, and we know that there is a world shortage of fertilizer. Then why put into the hands of one or two companies in this country a complete monopoly in the manufacture of fertilizer? With the price of fertilizer going up during the early part of the war, we have no guarantee that these people will not shove the price up still further as they did prior to the war.

My hon. friend says that they have put the price up. When was that? I understood it was Selling lower today than when the government was operating the plant. The fact of the matter is that the Calgary plant and the Trail plant were suitable for manufacturing ammonium nitrate, and the government by a happy invention devised a process for making a fertilizer from ammonium nitarte. Ninety-five per cent of this ammonium nitrate was sold outside Canada. Less than five per cent of the Calgary production was taken in Canada. It was not a fertilizer that western Canada ever uses. It is used a little in eastern Canada, mostly in the mari-times. Why we should hang on to the production of a chemical fertilizer that requires a world market, I cannot see. We did sell out the Calgary plant which developed this fertilizer, and we recovered from the plant more than w'e spent on building it; that is, the combined Trail and Calgary plants.
The Welland plant was built for the manufacture of picrite, one of the components of which is ammonia. Therefore we had a small ammonia unit in this plant. We converted that to making ammonium nitrate-, but the production was not sufficient to do any more than carry the plant. There were chemical features in there which should properly be used for industrial production in this country. It meant that we were laying off staff and getting down to an operating staff on the ammonium nitrate plant. Today it is a full-fledged chemical plant as it was designed to be, and will be maintained as such and keep up with the requirements of the times.
I have heard a good deal of talk about the sale of these plants, but I never heard one logical reason why they should not be sold. Remember this is not a socialist government that I am a member of. Why the government

Supply-Reconstruction and Supply
of Canada should operate government-owned plants to sell fertilizer around the world, I cannot see.
Then why did the minister commit himself?
If the hon. member will read the letter carefully he will see that I said there was no present intention of selling the plant. A year later I had an opportunity to sell it and I sold it.
What percentage of the cost did you get for it?
About twenty-five per cent of the cost of construction.
Have a by-election.

I do not want to have a by-election yet. In Chilliwack we have women in from the military camp of western Canada. Maternity cases are being looked after in our hospital at Chilliwack. In spite of that, we are asked1 to pay this high price. I want an explanation from the minister. He has not given me one yet.
The hon. member has not given me a chance.

I have been giving the minister a chance for three years, and. he has been writing letters or some of his officials have been writing letters that do not mean anything except to say that Prince George and Prince Rupert can have it because in one case the property is government owned and in the other case it is on leased1 property. I am asking for a better explanation than that. We have no by-election in Chilliwack; we do not intend to have one for some time; but I want to know why my riding is being discriminated against particularly when we have the one permanent army camp in western Canada.

All I can say about Chilliwack is this. The collection of huts my hon. friend is talking about happened to cost in excess of $300,000. They are offered to him at ten per cent of the cost, together with land and all appurtenances, which is $30,000. I have a note here which says that Mr. Sparling from our Vancouver office is on his way to Chilliwack now to go into the matter further to see if arrangements can be made.
My hon. friend talks glibly about the situation in Prince Rupert and in Halifax. I may say this about Halifax. Our only instructions to War Assets Corporation is to get the best recovery possible from any article of government property that is assigned to it for sale. If the town happens to own the property and it is on lease and the lease provides that the building is to be removed from the property and the property restored to its original value, I suppose the basis of the sale is exactly that, sold for removal, and naturally it is worth far less for removal than it is if you can use it on the ground on which it is built. We have been told by the experts during the past three years how we should sell this, that and the other thing. We do the best we can. I can assure my hon. friend that politics or

Supply-Reconstruction and Supply
sentiment or doing good to people have no part in the work of War Assets Corporation. It operates to get a fair return.

I am willing to concede that politics have no part in it. The minister told me that doing good has no part in it. A hospital is necessary for the district and that is not taken into consideration. I am told by the minister's own letters that this Jap camp at Tashme settlement was made for $27,000.
No.

Just a minute; it is under your own signature. You may have forgotten it, but I have not. They asked about $52,000 and a settlement was made for $27,000. The sum of S500 a month was paid in rent. The farm never paid that amount in a year in profit. The minister says that there is no sentiment attached to this hospital. I appreciate the fact that the minister has told me that Mr. Sparling is on his way to the district. I would suggest that Mr. Sparling look at things from a humanitarian point of view and not from War Assets point of view.

I should1 like to follow up the question asked a few moments ago by the hon. member for Leeds with which the minister did not deal. He asked for some indication as to when the work of War Assets Corporation could be wound1 up. I understand, from the annual report of the company which covers the twelve months ended March 31 of this year, that they are meeting with a great deal of difficulty now in carrying on their business. For example, on page 8 we find that a lessening of demand for surplus goods is now very apparent. Then on page 10 of the report says that the corporation is now entering into the period of comparatively small single sales. On page 11 it is stated that industry is reaching the end of the period of reconversion, and that this means also that surplus property will have to compete more actively with the products of private industry, and that disposal of surplus from now on will present more difficulty and yield a lower return. I take it that from now on we may expect less profit, less money realized from the transactions of War Assets Corporation, and at the same time expect high overhead. This evening the minister said the number of employees is still 8,000. That is about 2,000 more than the highest number during 1945-46, although it is some 2,000 lower than the highest figure during 1946-47. What about the future of this corporation? The total payroll given in the report is $15,624,905.31. I presume that was for the fiscal year, but it seems obvious that we shall have heavy

payroll and heavy expenditures with constantly diminishing returns. Can the minister give us some further answer to the question placed before him by the hon. member for Leeds?
This material has no value unless it is sold. If it has no value it is turned over to War Assets Corporation. I can assure my hon. friend that the cost-
That is hardly right. If it has no value it is not turned over to War Assets.
If it has no value to War Assets Corporation it is not turned over. What does my hon. friend suggest, that we start giving it away?
The minister need' not fly off the handle.
I am not flying off the handle; I am wondering-
I am asking him a question in a reasonable way and not with any attempt to get him into any kind of trouble. I think we are entitled to know something about the policy for the future.

At the moment the cost of doing business is about thirteen per cent of recoveries. The cost may rise. Naturally, if the sales get smaller and selling is more difficult the cost of sales will go up. We anticipate that another $50 million can be recovered from the sale of war assets. We will carry on as reasonably as we can and when the work is finished1, when the cost of sales is more than the value of sales, at an appropriate time we shall wind up the activities of the corporation.
Is the $50 million mostly in ships?
Oh, no.
Has there been a change recently in the policy of the corporation? Are they not changing the policy to meet changing conditions?
Yes.
Having regard to smaller sales and greater sales resistance?

Yes. We are having more branch sales. Branches are a higher proportion of the total than in the early stages. Industrial real estate is practically all sold. The ships are all sold. The items that offer large recovery for individual sale are gone. Sales today represent a great variety of material that is put on display in warehouses throughout 'the country. The public are asked to go and bid for them, but individual sales are today very much down. In April,

Supply-Reconstruction and Supply
1946, the average sale per invoice was $4,987.45, or practically $5,000 for each invoice. That diminished in December of the same year to $1,225.87. In January, 1947, it was down to $776, and in March it was $706.
Dropping all the time.
Yes.
Is the corporation going to continue with a large number of warehouses, or will the good be concentrated?

The warehouses are shut down progressively. The purpose is to concentrate on not more than one warehouse in each area. That practically means each province, treating .the maritimes as one province. We are working in that direction and when we get that down theoretically we shall try to retreat into one .warehouse at some central point. It is a contracting operation.

The minister mentioned individual sales. I am particularly interested in that, for the reason that I know several service men who wish .to obtain lathes and other machinery. What is the .policy? To what extent are individuals able -to buy in any of this material at the present time?
If a man wants to buy a lathe he buys it from the dealer. War Assets is not a retail business. It is not a .place for a man to go and spend $50. It is a wholesale business.

Am I to understand that there is no use in a service man making application for a certain amount of machinery in a certain place, for .the reason that it has been turned over .to War Assets and he has to go through the operation of buying it from a dealer? He cannot buy direct.

The
minister uses terminology to which apparently some of us attach different meanings. For example, he used the word "reasonable" in describing the policy of War Assets Corporation, but it seems to me that the whole policy is based on the theory that what is good for some people is not so good for others. I say frankly that I do not think it has been a very good policy for the Canadian people, and in this connection I should like to revert to the disposal of plants. I do not think there is really any point in referring to the fact that we do use a good deal of nitrate in Canada in fertilizers. I do not believe the minister would go to an eastern farmer or those in the west who use 11-48 fertilizer mix on their fallow wheat or on their potato crops and
tell them that it was not important or that the price should not be kept in line with cost of production and sale prices. I might say that up to date there has been no safeguard that I can see. My information is that already ingredients going into fertilizer mix are increasing. Pressure is being brought to bear for increased prices. The price of fertilizer today is such that, selling for $64 for 11-48 in my own province of Saskatchewan, the farmers cannot use it. The answer is, of course, that if you want soil conservation, if you want to increase and stabilize production, you have to start using this commodity. Here was an opportunity of keeping this product under public control where we could have had this main ingredient going into fertilizer, now that we have found potash in Saskatchewan and could have increased over-all production. I would point out that we have experimentation in process at the universities, and we should have a correlated plan with the Department of Agriculture so that our whole economy would work together, instead of having this hit-or-miss method that we are following. I cannot believe that the Minister of Agriculture was happy about the sale of these things. From the point of view of the agriculturist, it has been a really bad mistake.

May I ask the minister whether he has considered the policy which was followed in the United States for the sale of their war assets? If so, has he considered that policy for Canada? Briefly stated, it is this. They gave their ex-service men priority on any sale. They could go for the first few days, then educational institutions, then state and municipal governments and, finally, the general public. Each group had its date and the ex-service men had a priority to buy these goods.

We tried to devise a servicemen's priority but could not see any way of doing so. The servicemen's priority practically broke down the operation in the United States. They had about three or four disposal agencies before they got around to our process under War Assets Corporation, and in every case it was the servicemen's preference that tied up sales. Even the limited preference we had caused more trouble and delayed operations to a greater extent than any other feature of our programme.

Last year the minister made the same statement, that the United States government had come around to our system. I was in New York in November, 1946, long after the house closed, and they were still using the system I have briefly outlined

Supply-Reconstruction and Supply
tonight. Evidently they did go through with it and it did provide a priority for servicemen. All the serviceman had to do was to present his discharge papers and get into the sale. .

I should like to ask the minister how many motor launches or other craft have been sold to the school of arts and crafts of Rimouski, Quebec, what the sale price was in each case, and what were the terms of disposal What were they to be used for?

Personally I have never
heard of the school of arts and crafts in tihe province of Quebec and I cannot answer the question. The officers here have some vague recollection that a boat or two were sold to them. We can give the reply in the morning.

One
other question. In regard to ball-bearings, when we sat on the war assets committee last year this question arose. Can the minister indicate the value of all types of ball-bearings which were surplus at the end of the war, whom they were disposed to, and the price in each case?

I presume they were parts
of automobiles. Is that what the hon. member has in mind?

My
understanding was that a good many ballbearings were made of non-standard size. I know something about mechanics, and to me it seems ridiculous that for most of our war purposes apparently these various types of ball-bearings, which of course, are quite expensive, were made non-standard so that their disposal was of very little use in postwar construction, such as for going into automobiles and other types of construction. Maybe the minister could indicate why that was.

The ball-bearings may not
have been standard for domestic vehicles. I do not think anyone making a tank would worry very much whether he used ballbearings which were standard for some peacetime vehicles. He would use the bearings which were required to carry the load. The same would be true of other special army vehicles. I have no knowledge of the situation, but I can very well imagine that a great percentage of the ball-bearings used in war were not suitable for peacetime vehicles.

Anybody would know
that.

Earlier in the session I brought to the attention of the

minister several thousand tons of steel which had been used in producing wartime barbed wire for farmers in the country. The whole amount of steel that went into that production was wasted. It would have been better if a good deal less of that barbed wire had been made and if we had something that would be of some use now. The whole works is wasted. How long is it the intention to continue to make wartime barbed wire? Why not go back to standard barbed wire so that the farmers will have something when they buy it?

We do not know anything
about that. If there was any standard barbed wire made during the war, I presume it was shipped overseas. What the steel companies are making today would not be within the purview of the government.

I should like to know the cost or the amount of rent paid for the lease on each piece of property required for hospital purposes by any department of government during the war, the cost of building each hospital, and the price which each building or property was sold at. I do not expect the minister to give me that information tonight, but I should like to have it tomorrow morning.
I am afraid that the night shift is not working tonight. I shall be glad to get the information for my hon. friend as soon as it can be obtained.
I should like it before the minister's estimates are carried. If he cannot get it tomorrow morning, tomorrow afternoon or tomorrow night will do.

I should like to make what I believe to be a constructive suggestion to the minister. It is in connection with the advertising of war assets. I have pretty nearly every advertisement I have seen in the papers. It seems to me that the great majority of the articles offered for sale are more or less in the form of white elephants. It seems to me that if we had a greater volume of advertising in connection with articles which are really saleable and can be used by a great many people, it would make for much greater sales.
I have tried to keep track of the advertising, and yet I have not been able to find anything that is usable in my location.

It is not the practice to advertise articles that are originally sold to the trade. We advertise white elephants because we want to get rid of them at a good price. A lot of standard articles we advertise. But where there is an agency of War Assets Corporation in the area, anyone buying a standard

Supply-Reconstruction and Supply
article is expected to get in touch with the agency and place his order accordingly. Standard articles are usually sold in large batches. We advertise real estate and ships and nonstandard usable articles, but not standard ones.
Let us have a good buy once in a while so that we can get something.

There is one other thing I should like to bring to the attention of the minister. Earlier in one of the aviation magazines there was an article about the Mosquito aircraft stored at Cumberland, where they were being protected with a certain spray or film for future use. I have now been informed that those have been disposed of. Is that correct?

We have not disposed of any Mosquito aircraft. I am told that some of the Cromlin Mosquitoes have been declared surplus and are in process of being transferred to War Assets Corporation. I am informed that only one or two have been sold.

There was considerable consternation among the people around London as to just what was going on there. We were led to helieve that these aircraft were being preserved for future use. These men who were employed there and knew what was going on, said that the engines were removed. When a Mosquito has the engine removed, the air frame is no longer of any use, and it was thought they were being sold for a song. Until the engines were taken out, they were a going concern. It looked as though part of the move was just to get the motor out, then the aircraft could be declared surplus. And when they did not have a plane to put it in, they could declare the motor surplus.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Shall the item carry?
No, I should like to have an answer to my question.

The hon. member will appreciate the fact that he is asking the wrong minister about that. We get the plane after it is declared surplus, after the army has decided what it will do with it. It is not the function of War Assets Corporation to say what is surplus and what is not. The army tell us what is surplus.
I think the people got a raw deal. I will tell the minister that.
Did the minister ever have any aircraft from Great Britain or the European theatre declared surplus to him?

Not to my knowledge. I think arrangements were made with the United Kingdom for the exchange of certain aircraft in use there and for certain other aircraft to be produced. I believe there was an arrangement for the exchange of surplus aircraft in the United Kingdom for jet planes now being produced. As far as I know, no aircraft were declared surplus to War Assets in the United Kingdom.
I am glad to get that information. I have been bothering the minister about several things along that line, and I hope the jets arrive in Canada soon.
Can the minister say what the total cost was of operating War Assets for the last year?

While we are getting that figure, I might point out that the costs of operating War Assets Corporation include the cost of operating the Valleyfield repair depot and various costs which add to recovery costs, and which are an operating cost.
That would be included in this?
Yes, that would be included in this.
They would not be included in the statement of War Assets Corporation for the year?
I am afraid I shall have to get that information for the hon. member. Perhaps I can have it later this evening.
I would ask that the item stand until I get an answer to my question.

I think that is a bit unreasonable. The hon. member's question has nothing to do with departmental administration. This item has nothing to do with hospitals around the country. We shall have to get that information from the people who built the hospitals; that is, from the Department of National Defence.
If the minister's department does not have that information it is about time they found out who has it. Your department has to look after the disposal of the properties.
Yes.

Then I want these figures. It seems that some of these properties have been sold at ridiculous prices, maybe too high, maybe too low. How can we check on it if we have not the information? If the minister has not the information I do not think he has any right to come before the committee with his estimates.

5714	COMMONS
Supply-Reconstruction and Supply
Well, I am before the committee.
And I ask that the item stand until you get that information.
I don't agree.
I don't care whether you agree.

If it is necessary to divide the committee on it, we shall do so. I am willing to meet any reasonable request, but when an hon. member asks me to let an item covering departmental administration stand until I can get from another department of government the cost of certain, hospitals and then find from War Assets Corporation the amounts for which they were disposed, I think the hon. gentleman is being unreasonable.
Well, you may think it is unreasonable, but when you are asking me now to approve your estimates-
I am not asking you.

Just a minute. You may have disposed1 of property costing $50,000 or $100,000; according to your own figures some property cost $200,000. It may have been sold for $5,000, and then you are asking me to approve your estimates.
I am not asking you to approve anything.

Yes, you are; and you are trying, to get the people of my riding to pay $30,000 for some property, while at the same time you are selling a property that cost at least as much for only $2,500, and I do not think you have any right to have your estimates approved.
I am asking that they be approved, nevertheless.
And I am asking that the item stand.
The minister will let me have that information either this evening or tomorrow morning?
I have it now. The cost of doing, business of War Assets Corporation was $45,529,102.45. That was the cost for the year 1946.
The fiscal year?
Yes, the fiscal year 1946-47.
To March 31, 1947?
Yes.

That raises an interesting question, because

that amount is well on to half as much as you expect to realize during the whole current year. You said you expected to realize about $100,000,000. I observe that your staff is down by only about twenty per cent, or perhaps less, and it seems to me that the cost will not be down very much.
By the way, I want to say I have been thinking over the answer the minister gave me some little time ago, about selling all these hundreds of millions of dollars worth of goods with no record at all of the cost. He certainly did not convince me as to the reasonableness of what he was saying, and I doubt if he convinced himself. He made it perfectly clear that he did have the figures available for many of these larger items; and I think he agreed that on all kinds of standard items the figures could be easily obtained. Perhaps this is not a good time at which to do it, but I am going to say now that I think that is wrong, unless there are some points about it I do not understand. Before this war assets thing is finally wound up, I believe figures should be given which will enable us to come to some judgment. Let me say at once I hope I am not going to be unreasonable. I know that articles costing perhaps $100,000 may have to be sold in some cases for one or two or three per cent of their cost, but that is not the case with all kinds of other articles. As the minister has said, some are sold for ninety per cent of their cost and others are sold for more than their cost. I believe a great deal of information should be given, so that people of this country and we who do our best to help protect their interests may have some means of coming to a decision. At the present time we are like a lot of children, with nothing at all on which to base our judgment. The only measure of efficiency we have-and it is a very small one-is the percentage of cost in the department on the actual sales; and according to the figures we now have, they are spending something like $45,000,000 to recover an amount of about $100,000,000 which does not give a very good impression of the efficiency of the department.
That shows how misleading casual information can be.
I quite agree; that is why we want better information.

I can give a break-down of the operating cost; Receiving, classifying and warehousing surplus, $11,398,914.66. Reconditioning clothing and other surplus goods, $2,724,965.18.
My hon. friend will realize that we take scrap clothing from the army, put it through a plant,

mend it, recondition it, press it and sell it as usable goods. Perhaps that 82,000,000 would have brought about a recovery of 89,000,000 or $10,000,000. Demolition and disposal of nonsalvageable surplus, which means chiefly ammunition; $2,034,965.87. That is a cost from which there was probably some recovery, because, after we take out the explosive, we sell it, and after we decontaminate the shell we sell it for junk, but that is the demolition cost. Recovery from salvageable material from ammunition and explosives, which has to do with the item I just read, $1,066,132.20. Freight and handling, $505,840.31. Lease termination and property restoration expenses, $404,238.89. Miscellaneous expenses, including agents' commissions, technical services and consulting fees, $1,774,247.57.
Then here is an item. We or War Assets took over the ship-building programme as is and where is. In other words, if a ship were three-quarters completed it was declared surplus in that condition. If it were half completed or quarter completed it was declared surplus. It was decided to complete certain ships, because the sale value completed would be very much more than the cost of completion plus the sale value in the half completed state. In that year the government spent $11,139,141.47 in completing ships. Incidentally they included three motor ships which were sold to Canadian National Steamships. Then there was an amount of $4,951,558.25 spent to complete mutual aid. Those items account for the direct operating costs, out of the total of $45,000,000 while the administrative expenses, that is the cost of doing business by the corporation, amounted to .$9,528,880.05, which, on business of $220,000,000, would be about 4-35 per cent.

Still it is your whole cost that is of interest, surely. I am not necessarily criticizing that figure, because your recovery last year was very much larger. What is bothering me is that, on the face of it, I would have thought these operations which you describe, and which seem very reasonable but which cost such a lot, would not continue to be carried on to nearly the same extent, and the thing that struck me was that if one can gauge, it by the number of your employees, taking that as a rough and ready basis, you will have something like eighty per cent of the cost with only about one-half the recovery.

Our costs today are running
about thirteen per cent of recovery. They were only 4-5 per cent at the same time last year.

In a return to a question which I asked some months ago. I notice that the navy turned, over this year up to May 6, 1947, $32,000,000 worth of goods; the army turned over $12,000,000 worth, and the R.C.A.F., $32,000,000 worth. When you got those articles that would be their cost, but apparently no endeavour is made to keep a historical record. When you get actual delivery in your warehouses you set up your own value, and then you calculate on what you realize on your sales as applied to that value which you have on your books, or to the original cost?

We do not know the original cost. For instance, the army may turn over an encampment, and they would charge as part of its costs the cost of building roads, laying underground pipe, lease of buildings and so on. As we all know, the Department of Reconstruction and Supply was set up for a limited period, to function during the the reconversion period. During this session there have been frequent instances where duties of the department have been transferred to other departments. On June 23 there was an article in the OttawTa Citizen to the effect that the Department of Reconstruction was being disbanded, and that it would cease opera-

Supply-Reconstruction and Supply
tions about September 1. Can the minister tell the committee whether that article is correct and, if not, just what are the intentions with regard to winding up the department? He might also tell the committee to w'hat extent he is still exercising his overriding authority over other departments. In the setting up of this department he wras given wide powers, including the. right to override other ministers in certain respects. Is that right still being exercised and, if so, to what degree? Finally, will he tell the committee how many crown companies there are under his department and give us some idea of their activities?

The Department of Reconstruction and Supply has two functions, one of which is to liquidate Canada's war commitments. That work is nearing completion. The staff of the department has dropped from about 5,000 down to 600 at the moment. The department is responsible for all government housing programmes and also for certain crown companies. There are five, perhaps six of those companies, including Polymer. Eldorado, Canadian Arsenals, Park Steamships Co. Ltd., War Assets Corporation, Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and Wartime Housing Limited.
Just the five?
No, seven. There may be others, such as Wartime Shipbuilding, in process of being liquidated. These companies are all doing extremely well under able management.
When is it expected to wind up the department?
That is government policy which will be made known in due course. We do not go by what the Citizen says.
What about the overriding powers?
What clause is that?

The minister knows very well that under the act setting up his department he was given overriding powers with respect to other departments. Are those powers being exercised, or is he now minding only his own business?
The overriding powers exist only in the mind of the questioner. The Department, of Munitions and Supply, like every other department of government, attends to its own responsibilities.

It is not the Department of Munitions and Supply; it is the Department of Reconstruction and Supply. If I had the

statute here I could read the section to the minister. If he is not exercising those powers I do not want to put any foolish ideas into his head. I had better not say anything more about the matter.

In 1945 I attempted to obtain the steering wheel of the corvette Dundas for the Dundas sea cadet corps. I wrote to the Steel Company of Canada, which I understood had purchased the vessel from War Assets, but I was informed in a letter of November 22, 1945, that the corvette Dundas was not in Hamilton, that it had been sold to the Sarnia steamship company at Port Colborne. I was advised to write to Captain Scott Misener, president of that company, to secure the information I desired. I wrote to him, and on December 10, 1945, I received an answer stating that when the corvette was inspected in Hamilton harbour it was found that practically every item of movable equipment aboard, even to the extent of the wheel, the ship's bells, compasses, et cetera, had been removed. Some time ago the editor of the Dundas Star endeavoured to secure the same article on behalf of the Lions club, and he was given more or less the same information. A couple of years afterward, on April 9, 1947, the Hamilton Spectator carried a picture story, showing the hon. member for Hamilton East presenting the steering wheel of H.M.C.S. Dundas to the Prime. Minister. The information accompanying this photograph was to this effect:
The helmsman's wheel of the doughty little corvette Dundas has found a resting place in high honour even as workmen in Hamilton harbour slash away the plates of the once proud fighting ship and prepare them for feeding into scrap iron furnaces. The ship's wheel, presented to Prime Minister W. L. Mackenzie ICing, will be hung in his summer home at ICingsmere. The presentation was made by Thomas H. Ross, member of Commons for Hamilton East. The wheel was salvaged by the International Metal Company, which is scrapping a number of corvettes for the Steel Company of Canada.
One corvette Dundas was scrapped in Port Colborne in the winter of 1945-46. and I wonder if the minister can inform me if there were two corvettes bearing the name Dundas? The information I have is quite misleading, because the original Dundas was scrapped by the Sarnia Steamships Limited in 1945-46. Does the minister know whether there were two ships with that name?
I do not know.

With regard to this accounting method, which I might say from what we can see from this distance does not seem to be very satisfactory, I think some record should be made of the historical cost of the various items, even to the armed services. But surely in regard to war assets from other departments of the government, civil departments, the original cost should be set up on the books of War Assets Corporation. We are.

The place to get that is from the person who bought it. My hon. friend mentioned $147,000. The material for public works was what had been worn out in the service of the department. That cost $167,000 when new. For instance, we sell typewriters, and some of them are sold as junk and others are usable for their spare parts.
You have a good explanation if they were junk. What was the original cost? We are entitled to know that.

The president of War Assets told me that there are life rafts which have been declared surplus, and they have had to be pulled up from the bottom of lakes. It might be interesting to someone to know what they cost.
The minister speaks of recovery. Would that be net or gross recovery?
Gross recovery.
Where does War Assets get its monev to operate?
Its income is derived from a certain portion of its sales. Originally it was three per cent, more recently five per cent, and now it has been raised to ten per cent.
If it gets its income from a portion of its sales, that cannot be the gross recovery which the minister mentioned. Who gets that $400,000,000?
1 The Receiver General.

It is taken out before we turn the money over to the Receiver General. The first deduction is the actual operating expense, the cost of getting the article in a saleable condition. Very little of the $10,000,000 was spent. The purpose of the vote is to take care of spotty unemployment. It was anticipated by hon. members opposite-I think I was the only optimist in the house- that there would be considerable unemployment following the war, and the purpose of the $10,000,000 vote was to permit projects to be undertaken to relieve spotty unemployment. Over $500,000 has been spent. What was it spent on?

Small items. The money was refunded. The $10 million was intact at the end of the year. The majority of the items for which money was spent were later voted in the estimates of the department and refunded. I can give my hon. friend what the amounts were. An allotment of $25,000

was provided for an aircraft landing strip at Pentecote, P.Q.; landing facilities at Baie Comeau, P.Q.; $25,000; landing facilities at Forestville, P.Q., $25,000; Pickle lake airfield, $5,000; Red Deer river diversion project, surveys, $115,000; South Saskatchewan river project, surveys, $137,000; telephone line, Whitefish Falls to Kiilarney, $9,000; wharf extension, Manitoulin island, $23,000.; fisheries research board, research re fish oils, $12,500; Louisburg wharf, construction, $210,000; Giant Yellowknife road, Northwest Territories, $18,500; Diamond Drill exploration in bituminous deposits of northern Alberta, $50,000; Bank erosion survey, Squamish river, Vancouver, $2,000; road, Jakes Corner to Atlin, B.C., $15,000; Snare river power development, Yellowknife district, $200,000. Reports were filed here on both of these projects.

No planning has been done. A report has been filed here within the last few days.

No, he did not say that. He announced that -the re-port had been filed in this parliament for a $20 million or $40 million programme or something of that sort. If my hon. friend will read -the repor-t which is a study of the engineers, he -will get all the information there. I know nothing about it-
Y'ou are not familiar with it?

He told the house a short time ago that part of this $5 million would be used for the Red Deer, -the Bow river and the Medicine Hat irrigation projects. Does the minister know7 if any will be used for this purpose? I am all for it.
I am willing to argue the matter.

At this time I should like to bring to the attention of the minister an idea that I think should come under this item. The Department of Mines and Resources is carrying on an aerial survey this year of the Groundhog coal fields at the headwaters of the Skeena. Next year the department intends to put in a ground survey crew to see what there is up in these fields. They are just 150 miles from the coast, and, as the minister knows, we are getting short of coal on the coast, I should like to see some of this money go into that survey, so that we can speed it up, which the minister can do as he has done during the war. I should like to see a concentration of effort in that field, so that we would know what we have there and can speedily develop it. I bring it to the attention of the minister possibly because it will be relevant in the immediate future.

In connection with what the hon. member for Skeena has just said, within the last two months I have tried to arrange with the folks up in that country as to whether I could get up to the Groundhog ' coal fields or not. My information is that there is no passable road. If my hon. friend would ask for the construction of a road into that area I would say that it would be money well spent.

I understand that we are on item 570. The discussion has been businesslike tonight; hon. members have asked important questions, and the minister has answered them well. I want to give him a breathing spell. I want to tell you, Mr. Chairman, that it is no mean job to be the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply at the present time, and the minister deserves special congratulation upon the effort that he is making in handling a most difficult job, a job that is more difficult to handle than anything else. I am surprised that I have to rise at this late hour to tell him my appreciation, which I hope is shared by many others. I do not always agree with the minister, but I am in full sympathy with him and I appreciate all the constructive criticism which comes from both sides of the house. But it seems to me that the minister is deserving of a special tribute for his efforts to improve reconstruction in this country. There are many obstacles in the way,

Housing development, including commitments of previous years-to provide for payments of amounts owing under guarantees pursuant to item 60 of schedule A to the Appropriation Act, No. 6, 1946 (and pursuant to corresponding items in previous Appropriation Acts) to approved lending institutions in respect of loans made for the purpose of financing the conversion of existing houses into multiple family houses, such payments to be made out of unappropriated moneys in the consolidated revenue fund, $250,000.

This item is preceded 'by the general description:	"housing development, including commitments of previous years", and! then follow about half a dozen items bearing on different housing expenditures. I want to take up a remark made by the minister in the debate last Saturday morning, July 12, on his estimates, which will be found on page 5517 of Hansard, and which contains an amazing statement. The minister said:
The government takes no responsibility for solving the entire housing problem for this country. It is perfectly ridiculous to suggest that it is government responsibility. Every city has its own housing responsibility as has every province. The government is responsible for the returned men and its responsibility stops at that point.
The statement, with which I take issue, is the concluding one:	"the government is
responsible for the returned men." Yes, of course, we are all agreed on that; but the minister proceeds to say:
And its responsibility-
That is the responsibility of the government with respect to housing.
-stops at that point.
I take complete issue with that statement. In the first place, I point out that it runs counter to the legislative action taken by parliament ever since 1935. Long before there was a war; long before there was a problem of housing in connection with returned men; long before that was even thought of, parliament had taken action recognizing a federal responsibility with respect to housing conditions in Canada. That recognition was given in the clearest terms in the National Housing Act of 1944. If the position the minister now takes is a valid one, then the government of which he was a member in 1944 had no business bringing in a national housing act. On his own reasoning, they had no business bringing in that act, and I am sure that
Mr. Pouliot.]
neither he nor any other member opposite will argue in support of that position.
In the second place, the position now taken by the minister is an absolute disavowal of the promises made by this government in 1945 in the general election campaign of that year, when they sought re-election. There was not the slightest suggestion in those days about fobbing off the responsibility for housing conditions in Canada on the local or provincial authorities. The government was lavish with its promises looking toward the correcting and curing of housing conditions in Canada, which were then presenting a problem in its incipient stages, which problem has grown to great proportions since. The present Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley) in that campaign came to Toronto and talked freely about all the houses that would be built within the twelve months after V-E day.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: And they were built.
The propaganda machine of the government was glib in talking about the 600.000 houses that would be built.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I said, that 50.000 houses would be built and they were built.
Stick to the facts.
I was speaking about the promises the government made. The present Minister of Justice made the promise that 50.000 houses would be built in the first twelve months after Y-E day.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: And it was done.

There was no talk then about the government having a limited responsibility with respect to housing conditions. The Minister of National Health and Welfare talked in glowing terms about the drive for tanks becoming the drive for houses; and there was no limitation of responsibility there, no talk about this being a local or provincial responsibility. There was glowing talk; there were glowing promises, about the construction of from 600,000 to 1,000.000 houses by the government. There was no talk then about these limitations in respect of the housing responsibility of the federal government; no talk of that responsibility being confined to the housing of veterans. It. was on these promises that the government got itself elected in 1945. If it had offered the kind of statement the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply

Supply

Reconstruction and Supply
made here last Saturday morning they would not be occupying the treasury benches here at the present time.
Xo man.talks so carelessly or inaccurately about housing as the hon. gentleman now on his feet, or so constantly.

There is another example of the way in which the Minister of Reconstruction rides roughshod over the rules of the house. He did not get up to ask a question but to make a statement which he cannot justify. He does not like to have me remind him about the promises the government made, and I say that his statement last Saturday represented a complete reversal of the promises on which this government got itself elected in 1945.
May I ask the hon. member a question?

No. j'ou cannot. I am sorry. I had enough of the hon. gentleman's interruptions recently in the public accounts committee. They were so utterly senseless that I will not waste my time on similar interruptions now. Time is too precious at this juncture of the session.
It is a fair question-

The government talks freely about what it claims to have accomplished, but about ninety per cent of it has been accomplished by private enterprise. The government takes full credit for it; but there is no suggestion, when my hon. friends are making these glowing claims in regard to performance, about the responsibility being divided or the credit being divided with the provincial and local governments. W7hen it comes to claiming, credit the federal government claims the full credit. If they claim the credit, they will have to take the responsibility that goes with it.
Not only that, but there is a fourth factor in the situation and it is this. This government, hanging on to power it grasped under the national emergency legislation, is the one government that has been possessed of all the powers that were necessary to enable it to cope with the housing crisis in Canada.
May I ask the hon. member a question?
Can you keep the hon. gentleman quiet, Mr. Chairman? If he cannot possess his soul in patience, deal with him as he ought to be dealt with.
Don't be so offensive.
To continue, Mr. Chairman-
If wind could build houses you would build lots of them.
I did not hear the hon. member.
If wind could build houses j'ou would build lots of them.

Anyone can make remarks of that kind, and I do not know anyone who has befuddled the question of the government's relationship to federal responsibility more than the Minister-of Labour. I well remember when his department possessed all the powers that any department of labour could possess or could ask for, he was trying to excuse the failure of this government to take action and get down to brass tacks in the Ford Windsor strike a j'ear and a half ago, bj' saying, "It is not our responsibility; it is the responsibility of the provinces." When this government had taken all powers from the provinces under the guise of national emergency, that was the excuse of the minister. We will not waste more time on the Minister of Labour.
On these four grounds, Mr. Chairman, I submit to you that what the Minister of Reconstruction is saj'ing does not fit the facts, but is a complete reversal of government promises, and the position he is now taking represents a callous turning of the government's back on the responsibility which is property that of the federal administration.
When we come to individual items I shall have more questions to ask. I want to ask some questions particularly about the item with regard to Wartime Housing Limited, but the minister has taken his departure.

speechtext:
No, he has not. Don't
put that on Hansard.

Out of all this welter of promises, in view of the confusion that exists in its various schemes, I say that it is time the government got down to brass tacks and told the committee exactly what the situation is. The last time we had a debate on housing I asked the minister to state what the immediate housing emergencj- shortage is in Canada to date. On July 22 of last year he made a statement in which he admitted-it was an amazing confession-that, in spite of the glowingly optimistic assertions he had made only a few months before, the emergency shortage of housing units on March 31, 1946, was
150.000,	and that even if Canada built 60,000 houses in the fiscal year ending March 31, 1947, the shortage would rise to 180,000, increasing by twenty per cent, by March 31, 1947.

Where did you get that?
